subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as Hon. Members are aware, the Financial Administration Act requires that statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament in order for the government to increase its outstanding debt. Specifically, Part IV, Section 36 of that Act requires that "no money shall be borrowed or security issued by or on behalf of Her Majesty without the authority of Parliament". This refers to new money only rather than the refinancing of existing debt since Section 38 of the Act provides continuing authority to borrow funds to repay maturing debt. Thus, statutory borrowing authority must be obtained from Parliament to permit the government to implement a regular debt program to meet its financial requirements.
Section 39 of the FAA, however, provides for the Governor in Council to authorize the borrowing of money if it appears that funds will not be sufficient to meet disbursements from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. This action is designed for short-term, temporary use only as the term of the borrowing may not exceed six months and each such borrowing requires approval by the Governor in Council.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to outline for the House the terms of the borrowing bill. The bill is structured to establish the principle that borrowing authority each fiscal year will be equal to the financial requirements plus a non-lapsing reserve. Given the uncertainty over the exact timing of the passage of the bill, it is also structured to ensure that the amount of authority available is always equal to this amount, regardless of when the Bill is passed. I will go over each clause in the Bill now.
Paragraph 2(1) of the Bill requests borrowing authority in the amount of $25.3 billion for fiscal 1988-89. This amount is equal to the $22.3 billion in financial requirements forecast in the budget plus a $3 billion non-lapsing reserve to cover contingencies such as a further build-up in official international reserves during fiscal 1988-89. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, you will see that The Fiscal Plan tabled this week is very clear in that respect.
Paragraph 2(2) states that all unused borrowing authority granted by the Borrowing Authority Act 1988-89, to the extent that the unused authority exceeds $3 billion, will be cancelled on March 31, 1989. This paragraph preserves the government's non-lapsing reserve to be carried forward into the next fiscal year and also ensures that $3 billion is the maximum amount to be carried forward.
Paragraph 3 states that any borrowing authority granted last year by the Borrowing Authority Act 1987-88 will be cancelled on March 31, 1988 or on the date that the new bill comes into force, whichever is later. Thus, this paragraph prevents the non-lapsing reserve granted for earlier years from accumulating but ensures that cancellation takes place at a time that is not disruptive to the implementation of the regular debt program.
Paragraph 4 ensures that if the new Bill is passed after March 31, 1988 and part of the non-lapsing reserve granted for 1987-88 is used, this amount will be deducted from the authority granted for 1988-89 and thus the total amount of borrowing authority available for the new fiscal year is not increased.
The borrowing Bill for 1988-89 is basically the same as the one for last year. As I said earlier, the amount requested is equal to the financial requirements plus a $3 billion nonlapsing reserve, once again, the same as last year. The new clauses, which I outlined above, simply ensure that these are the amounts available, regardless of when the bill is passed.
For the information of Hon. Members, Mr. Speaker, I would now like to review how the borrowing authority granted for the current 1987-88 fiscal year had been used to the end of January. For 1987-88 a total of $25.8 billion was granted, made up of $21.3 billion, an amount equal to the financial requirements forecast in February 1987, a $3 billion reserve and $1.5 billion provided a separate supplementary borrowing authority Bill for 1986-87. This latter amount was carried forward to enable $600 million of Treasury bills issued pursuant to Section 39 of the FAA in the 1986-87 fiscal year to be rolled over in the current fiscal year and to cover the

February 12, 1988
Borrowing Authority
delivery of $900 million of Canada bonds delivered in April, 1987 but sold in March, 1987 pursuant to Orders in Council granted in March, 1987, charging the issue of these bonds to borrowing authority granted for 1986-87,
To the end of January, domestic and foreign borrowing programs had used about $14.8 billion of the authority granted for 1987-88. Of this amount, about $7.8 billion was charged to the marketable bond program and $9.7 billion to the issue of Canada Savings Bonds. Over the same period the amount of Treasury bills outstanding was reduced by about $2.5 billion and about $0.2 billion of outstanding foreign debt, on balance, was redeemed. The reduction in the amount of outstanding Treasury bills to the end of January was the result of the large CSB sales last fall and the consequent need to reduce cash balances to more normal levels. Over the remainder of the fiscal year, net Treasury bills sales are expected to pick up substantially to finance the government's borrowing requirements. Over the fiscal year as a whole, the amount of borrowing authority remaining at the end of March, 1988 is expected to be somewhat less than $3 billion. Thus, foreign exchange transactions, which to the end of January had increased official foreign exchange reserves from the beginning of the fiscal year, and had to be financed through the sale of Canadian dollars, are expected to have used a portion of the reserve granted for 1987-88.
However, as Hon. Members know, these foreign exchange transactions have been large and volatile in the past and the situation could change considerably before the end of the fiscal year.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to remind Hon. Members that it is most important that the government be in a position to maintain an orderly ongoing debt program and to minimize uncertainty in the capital markets. Expeditious passage of this Bill will help to achieve these objectives.

Mr. Speaker, we are here today to debate borrowing authority Bill C-109 after the presentation of a quite extraordinary so-called Budget which in fact was 95 per cent electioneering and self-congratulation on the part of the Government, with remarkably little content. The Government is asking us to give it authority to borrow over $25 billion but the Estimates will not be coming forward until about 10 days from now, so that we are being asked to approve a blank cheque with no idea of how this money will be spent. Certainly the Budget we saw yesterday gives us very little idea of how the money will be spent. Therefore, when the Parliamentary Secretary asks for such an important Bill to be passed quickly, he is asking for something that is totally unrealistic. The Official Opposition will be responsible. We certainly will not hold up the Bill unduly but we want to see the Estimates and we will want to have some careful examination of Government spending plans.
A well-known journalist wrote the other day that the trouble with the Budget, which is a paean of praise to the ruling Party, is that it strains credulity to the limit. Wrapped around one simple fiscal measure, a gas tax increase, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has managed to work a whole Tory election manifesto. Its message, repeated endlessly in numbing detail, is that those we elected in 1984 have been better financial managers than those before them.

He continues that if the Government of the day is going to produce a Budget that is 95 per cent electioneering guff and 5 per cent serious content, it is setting itself up for a few querulous voices to be raised in dissent. I think most of us would agree except we would say that it is not only querulous voices that will be raised in dissent but voices of reason which will be asking for the facts that were not in the Budget produced the other day.
The Government is asking for authority to borrow $25.3 billion, too much for a Government which has not delivered on its promises to Canadians not to raise taxes and to lower the deficit. The Minister of Finance, in his budget speech, said the deficit had been reduced to $29.3 billion. However, this is the result of a lot of smoke and mirrors. Some very creative accounting has been used to create the illusion that the public debt has been lowered when in fact it is higher.
The second point I want to repeat is that the Main Estimates will not be tabled until February 23, 1988, so we are being asked to vote on this Bill on faith. This Budget does not inspire confidence. In fact, the Budget brought down Wednesday, as my colleague, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) pointed out, is not even a proper Budget. A Budget usually sets out a Government's philosophy, policy and plans, but the Government wasted time and energy to produce a package of self-serving, self-congratulatory, repetitious rhetoric on what the Government is alleged to have done for Canadians since 1984.
Not one of Canada's economic problems has been solved. This budget puffery and self-congratulation is an insult to poorer Canadians, older workers, senior citizens, the unemployed and the homeless. The Government has left those people out of the Budget and misled those Canadians it hoped to reassure with its puffed-up rhetoric.
I want to return to the illusory $29.3 billion deficit which in fact is probably closer to $32 billion or $33 billion. One of the accounting tricks used is that of accelerated remittances. Canadian employers who must deduct income tax, unemployment insurance premiums and Canada Pension Plan contributions from their employees and remit those deductions to the Government have been steadily required to do it more often. Starting January, 1987, instead of remitting the deductions once a month they became obliged to remit them twice a month. That gives the Government a once-only increase in cash flow of $1.6 billion. The figures look better at the end of
February 12, 1988

the financial year because the Government has one additional fortnightly payment, but that is not a real saving.
Subsequently the Government moved to require employers to remit weekly, a further one-time increase in their cash flow, but not a real reduction in expenditures in any way. The Government has also postponed certain expenses such as spending on defence. In addition, the Government has given itself a six-month interest free loan in that although certain income taxes have been reduced as of January of this year the payroll deductions do not in fact take effect at the new rate until July. Therefore, employers are still remitting to the Government at the old unreduced rate. That gives the Government, in effect, an interest-free loan for this year of something in the order of $1 billion.
No less an authority than the Bank of Montreal said in one of its recent publications that if you take away all this creative accounting the public debt should be about $4 billion higher than the figure quoted by the Minister of Finance of $29.3 billion.
The Government has raised taxes at a rate higher than that of any Government since Confederation.

As I was saying, the Government has raised taxes more than any Government before it since Confederation. It continues the process. The Budget we heard on Wednesday had one additional tax measure which showed. I will return to the hidden ones, but the one that showed was another one cent a litre increase in gasoline tax effective April 1, 1988. In all, that makes an increase of 23 cents a gallon since 1984.
We also heard the announcement about the new rules for calculating federal sales tax, another band-aid mechanism that will not end the problem of disparity in tax rates across industries and the bias against exports.
The Minister has been holding forth about manufacturers sales tax for a long time. He has described it as a killer of jobs. Nevertheless, he keeps increasing the base and the rates. He tells us that at some date in the future he will replace the
Borrowing Authority
manufacturers sales tax with a new consumption sales tax. Meanwhile, as he inveighs against it, he increases its use.
1 want to describe briefly some of the increases in taxes which we have seen since the Government came in. Some of them are built in so that they increase year after year. The most important one, of course, was the deindexation of the tax system. This continues year after year. At the same time as the Government reduces the payments for family allowances, child deductions, and spousal allowances-tax measures that are particularly useful to young families with young children-the personal exemption on income taxes has had indexation removed from it. This means that there is built-in forever and ever a steady increase in the tax system. This year alone it is worth $750 million to the Government although all the selfcongratulation in the Budget speech did not mention that.
The Minister criticizes the manufacturers' sales tax so much, but look at the way he has used it since he came to power. On October 1, 1984, it was increased from 9 to 10 per cent. On January 1, 1986, it was increased from 10 to 11 per cent. On April 1, 1986, it was increased from 11 to 12 per cent. The impact on tax revenues was a $3 billion gain to the Government as a result of those.
On July 1, 1985, we saw the sales tax extended to candy and soft drinks. On July 1, 1987, we saw the sales tax extended to fast food and snacks. Those two measures netted the Government $460 million. On January 1, 1988, we saw sales tax increased from 8 to 12 per cent on paint, wallpaper, and toys. That measure gets the Government $60 million a year. The increase in gasoline excise tax of 2 cents a litre on September 3, 1985, brought the Government $900 million a year. The one cent a litre increase on January 1, 1987, and the one cent a litre increase on February 9, 1987, each brought the Government $450 million a year. That is before yesterday's increase.
We have seen progressive increases in air transportation taxes since May 1, 1986, which have netted the Government $55 million. There have been increases in duty on alcohol and tobacco; the first May, 1985, the second February, 1986, and another in January, 1988.
The Government continues to increase taxes while not lowering the public debt. On January 1, 1988, we had a 10 per cent tax on long distance telephone calls and cable television services. That will bring the Government $945 million a year. We saw the elimination of the Registered Home Ownership Savings Plan in May, 1985. The Government gained $105 million from that. We saw a permanent 3 per cent surtax on all taxpayers applied on July 1, 1986, and that continues. Many people think that it ceased at the same time as the 5 and 10 per cent surtax on high income earners ceased in December, 1986, but not so. That surtax is still in place. The Government has taxed Canadians to the hilt but is not reducing spending.
Let us look at some examples of what the Government spends its money on. We saw the bail-out of the Canadian Commercial Bank and Northland Bank, and the cost of the

Estey Commission set up to examine the Government's poor decision, $1.6 billion and climbing.
The cost of the Stevens inquiry was $2.3 million. New uniforms for the Armed Forces amounted to $2.7 million, which is not an expense anyone would grudge if they were good quality, but we hear complaints that the uniforms smell.
The salaries and office expense of Canadian trade negotiator, Simon Reisman is $10 million over three years. However, in order to promote this deal there is a $12 million campaign to persuade Canadians of the value of something which is quite questionable.
The budget for Cabinet Ministers' staff doubled under the Government. The new cost is $15.1 billion a year.
The Shamrock Summit in Quebec cost $2.6 million. While I am sure the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) sang nicely, 1 question whether it did anything else for Canada.
Office renovations for Conservative Ministers have come to $107,500 since they first took power. Redecoration of certain Ministers' offices amounts to $425,201.
We then come to the Prime Minister's travels. A trip to Asia in May, 1986, cost $1 million, including $3,500 for the butler and maid, and $150,000 for the sound and video equipment. There is $492,000 minus $28,000 that still must be accounted for.
There was a shadow aircraft flying alongside the Prime Minister's airplane to Baie Comeau in July and to Toronto in August, which cost $1,900 an hour. Executive jet bills run up by the Conservative Government in the first 45 days in office amounted to $345,000. I could go on and on with the list. The fact is that the Government's behaviour in office does not inspire confidence and certainly does not justify it coming in without the Estimates, asking to have its borrowing Bill passed on faith.
Since the forecast for the 1987-88 fiscal year was last given in the June, 1987 White Paper, budgetary expenditures have grown by $1.1 billion, in spite of the fact that almost $1 billion less than anticipated was paid out in unemployment insurance benefits. There is $2 billion in increased public debt charges from a government that undertook to reduce the public debt.
Both the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) said before and after they came to office that taxes would not be increased, yet taxes and spending have increased at an almost unbelievable rate.
The Minister congratulated himself generously in his Budget Papers for the fact that some aspects of the economy are better than expected. These congratulations do not belong to the Government. The improved state of our economy in some respects is due to the fact that we are in the sixth year of recovery from a cruel and almost unbelievably harsh worldwide economy. Of course, the Government inherited certain sound building blocks from the previous government which had managed an extraordinarily difficult recession in a way designed to reduce, as much as possible, the hardship on Canadians. Furthermore, the Government has benefited from a change in Canadian habits. Canadians used to be great savers but are now consuming more. The Government and the economy have certainly benefited from increased consumer activity.
In summary of my criticisms of the Budget and the Government's performance to date, I suggest that we have a Government that has taxed and spent. Taxes are increased and the public debt is increased. It is a Government that has not shown much concern for low and middle income Canadians. It has been particularly hard on young families with children, who are bearing the brunt of most of the Government's policies.
Since 1984 individuals have seen both their personal and sales taxes increased by $29.3 billion, or 68 per cent. Corporations have had their taxes increased by 28 per cent, or $2.6 billion. Even after so-called tax reform, 60,000 profitable corporations still pay no tax. Yet what does this mean to the average family? A family of four with a single earner and an income of $32,000 has faced a total tax increase since 1984 of $1,200 per year. There is very little for the average income family to correct the inequities of previous Budgets and the White Paper exercise in tax reform.
The Government has taken some steps to increase the lot of the very poorest, those with incomes of under $20,000 a year, but those with incomes between $20,000 and $40,000, especially if they have children and there is a spouse who is not working outside the home, are carrying the main brunt of the Government's policies.
With all those conditions, I think it is absolutely ridiculous for the Government to come in with a request to borrow over $25 million with no Estimates and ask us to vote for that Bill today on faith. When we see the Estimates on February 23 and have some idea of exactly how the Government proposes to spend the money that Canadian taxpayers have had extracted from them, we will be in a better position to decide on this Bill.
The Government continues to boast about the job creation figures. Those figures have, of course, improved, as they should have in the sixth year of recession. We still have over a
February 12, 1988

million Canadians unemployed and the Government appears to have abdicated its responsibility to them. Programs for job creation are steadily being cut. We are told that the economy is so good people should be able to find jobs without any assistance from the Government. That is true in certain regions. It is certainly not true in all parts of Canada and it is certainly not true for the young, whose unemployment rate continues to be twice the national average, and for people over 50 who are displaced for any reason and who find great difficulty getting into retraining programs.
We have a Budget before us that addresses the future in an entirely inadequate way in at least two respects, first, in its treatment of the deficit, which has been less than honest and, second, in its forecast for the Canadian economy, which is all smoke and mirrors.
In the tone of incredible self-congratulation which runs through these Budget books, we find the Minister is even comparing himself with the Olympic athletes. He invites all Canadians to emulate the Olympic athletes gathered in Calgary. He stated their commitment and quest for excellence must be what we as a nation bring to the task of building our economy. That is a fine sentiment. Is the Minister prepared to put some action behind that sentiment?
Two years ago we had a budget that told us that the deficit would come down in stages, to $27.9 billion in the fiscal year 1989-90, $25.8 billion in 1990-91 and $23.5 billion in 1991-92. That was what the Minister said. It was in his papers. He is now showing a $28.6 billion deficit for 1989-90 and, as I said, that also depends on creative accounting. The real figure is probably nearer $32 billion.
The Minister of Finance in his Budget papers also included one thick document entitled The Fiscal Plan, but it gives no detailed figures after the next two years. What kind of planning is that? We used to have a five-year plan. In fact, we were led to understand there would be a five-year forecast. This document tells us, without giving us any detail, that by 1992-93 the deficit will have shrunk to $19.5 billion. It does not tell us how this will be achieved. It is another statement of faith.
Furthermore, the Minister talks about an improving employment situation but traditionally we have needed to see 3 per cent growth in the economy just to stand still in terms of job creation. The Minister anticipates 3 per cent growth or better from now until 1993, but other economic forecasters see lower growth, more around 2.5 per cent. So it goes, on and on.
Unfortunately, the Department of Finance projections appear so rosy that one has to take them with some skepticism. There are very few solid figures in any case. There is a great deal of puffery. We have five documents, in all about 18 inches thick, to announce one tax measure, an increase of a penny a litre on gasoline and one cut of $300 million in Government services somewhere-we are not told where. We have to wait for a Treasury Board announcement to see when, where and how. For those two announcements we received about 10
Borrowing Authority
pounds of paper, essentially of a self-gratulatory description- less than accurate-of the Government's term in office. This Budget is an electioneering document prepared at the expense of the taxpayers. It is less than honest.
On the basis of that, and no Estimates, we are being asked to give the Government borrowing authority of $25.3 billion today. I am sure you can see, Mr. Speaker, that while the Government has to be able to transact its business-even if we think it is transacting it less than efficiently, as a responsible Official Opposition we will certainly not hold up the borrowing authority indefinitely-we do want to see the Estimates. We want to scrutinize the expenditures. We want a little more time to examine the tables which were published with the Budget papers, such as they were. The information was limited. Some of it is contradictory. My Party will have other speakers today on this Bill, but we will not be holding up the Bill unduly. However, we certainly would want to see the Estimates before it is passed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased today to speak on Bill C-109, an Act to provide borrowing authority. As the previous speaker said, we do not have the official Estimates so we do not have the details of exactly how this money will be spent and exactly where the cuts will be in the non-statutory programs as outlined in the Minister's Budget this week. Therefore, it is very difficult to comment on the $25.3 billion which is being sought under this borrowing authority Bill. We are aware that it is necessary for the business of the Government to carry on, but the only indicaters we have from the Government of where it is intending to go with this was in the Budget speech this week.
I would like to make a few references to the Budget and to look at a few areas where, perhaps if there had been more targeted spending, more efficient spending, the need for authority to borrow so much would not be required.
My Party along with many Canadians, waited with great excitement and anticipation for the Budget which came out this week. We expected strong measures to attack many of the issues of the day, such as regional disparities and cutting the deficit. This borrowing Bill certainly indicates that we need to continue to pay our debts and that the debts are not going to go down by very much.
Some of us had hoped that this Budget would take a strong stand, that we would be able to reduce our deficit by realigning some priorities the Government has outlined in previous papers, for example, by rejecting huge expenditures of billions of dollars for such large ticket items as nuclear submarines, which are of dubious value. Perhaps we could look at something more realistic and more in line with what is really needed for the protection of our sovereignty and the defence of Canada.
We had hoped to see some innovative measures which would have increased tax revenues thereby reducing the need for such

February 12, 1988
Borrowing Authority
a large amount of borrowing. Increasing the number of taxpayers increases the amount of revenue. We had hoped to see very strong measures to attack regional unemployment which would have put the over 1 million unemployed back to work, thereby increasing the number of taxpayers.
We have not seen the Estimates so we do not know exactly how all of these funds will be allocated. What we saw instead in the Budget is lost opportunities. It fails to raise tax revenue from corporations and it fails to get people back to work. In the Budget we see that the Government has decided to hold its course.
At first, when we looked at the Budget many of us thought it was a sort of ho-hum, couch potato type of Budget. There was nothing in it worth getting up off the couch to turn off the TV and watch. When one considers the amount of money that the country is having to borrow under this Bill, we know that we are in very serious trouble. The biggest problem will be the legacy left for the next Government after this obvious preelection Budget. Of course, Members of the NDP are pretty worried about, that given that it is most likely that we will form the next Government.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party has raised some very serious concerns about the trade agreement and economic union with the United States that this trade agreement causes. When we look at the Budget we can see what we are losing in revenues, which relates to the amount of money we have to borrow. Lost revenues obviously necessitate the borrowing of more money. In looking at the Budget we see that the Government has estimated it will lose $55 million in revenue owing to the bilateral agreement in 1988-89. On top of that we will lose $460 million in 1989-90 because of this bilateral trade agreement.
Jane Taber of The Ottawa Citizen in an article yesterday estimated that these losses will continue to increase as a result of the trade agreement. She estimates that they will increase to about $2.5 billion by 1999 when the deal will be fully implemented.
Under the seemingly benign heading of "Changes due to economic and other factors" the Government also projects a loss in revenue from unemployment contributions by $15 million in 1988-89 to a whopping $440 million in 1989-90. I might be pretty new to the House but it seems to me that what that says is just what Members of the New Democratic Party have been saying all along, that is, that the Government anticipates a significant decrease in employment in the next two years.
In this respect we have to consider again the trade agreement and the economic union with the United States. If this were not the case then why would contributions to unemployment insurance decrease? They can only decrease because people are not working or because they are making lower wages.
If one looks carefully at this one part of the Bill, one will see that we are projecting very high losses in revenue from the bilateral agreement and that obviously the Government is anticipating significant decreases in employment up until 1990. This causes us to observe that the trade agreement with the United States looks less free each day. This borrowing Bill confirms that it is not so free, which leads me to my next point.
The Budget fails to meaningfully address regional disparity. If the Government had come up with proposals to attack some of the problems connected with regional disparities, there may have been less of a need for such a high amount of borrowing. In this respect I want to give some concrete examples with respect to the number of people unemployed.
1 am talking here about the 19.6 per cent of the people of Newfoundland who are unemployed, the 11.4 per cent of the people of British Columbia who are unemployed and the 9.7 per cent of the people of Quebec who are not working. I am talking about the 13.7 per cent of the people of New Brunswick who are not working. These people are not paying any taxes. This is why I say that the Government has lost the opportunity to bring forward some innovative measures to raise revenue.
Despite the Government's self-congratulatory comments on how many jobs it has created, that is of little comfort to the almost 20 per cent of Newfoundlanders who are unemployed. There was an important statistic left out of the Government's self-congratulatory message. According to Statistics Canada, there were more bankruptcies in Canada in 1987 than in any year since 1984. In 1987 the largest number of people and businesses went bankrupt, any they were not paying any taxes. The number in this respect was 24,348. Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the effect on families and individuals of those bankruptcies? We only see the statistics. We do not see what is really happening to the families and to those people the statistics represent.
There was an opportunity to really attack regional disparities, to ensure that people everywhere would be working, and working meaningfully. One of the best ways to bring this about would have been to ensure that the economic development programs that exist for the regions were included in this measure. We have to raise a question about that. In its regional policy, as outlined by the Minister, the Government mentions three things; the Western Diversification Fund, the Atlantic Opportunities Fund and the Northern Ontario Fund. So far those are nothing but names. We do not see what they will be doing. These programs do not address the needs of northerners, or the needs of many others in the northern parts of other provinces who are often in equally disadvantageous positions. Southern Ontario seems to be presented as a place that is really making it, where everyone is doing well. Even in southern Ontario in some places, such as Windsor, the unemployment rate is 14 per cent.
I see that my time is up for the moment, Mr. Speaker. I would like to continue my remarks later if I may.
February 12, 1988

subsubtopic: PRESENCE OF CONVICTED AIRCRAFT HIJACKER IN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this week in Montreal the Government is sponsoring a conference on airport terrorism. This follows a very good initiative launched many years ago by Pierre Trudeau. Ironically, at the same time there is a terrorist present in Canada who got here through a series of bungles. While the Government is attempting to deport him, or stating that it is, it is not following the most expeditious means at its disposal to do so. I have asked questions about this matter and received pretty unsatisfactory answers.
I am wondering why the Attorney General of Canada (Mr. Hnatyshyn) has not taken the initiative of charging this individual, under Section 6 of the Criminal Code, with the offence of hijacking. This is a relatively new section of the Act. Because that individual has been charged and convicted in another country, he has not been dealt with within the meaning of the treaty because he did not serve his full sentence. I would hope that the Attorney General would consider that recourse.

Mr. Speaker, on March 19, 1975, journalist Armand Beaudoin wrote an article in VEcho Abitibien under the heading: CN's lousy service-Merchants up in arms, in which he said: "At CN, the whole attitude has become so negative that nobody knows what is happening. We think the people responsible for this situation are in Montreal."
Things are the same today, Mr. Speaker. We are all fighting to keep CN in Abitibi. CN could increase its market share by 28 per cent. CN is viable in Abitibi-Temiscamingue.
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask the President of CN, Mr. Lawless, to appoint immediately a permanent district manager in Senneterre. We also want to see Mr. Lawless in Senneterre a few weeks from now, to meet with Mayor Denis Sawyer and
members of the Senneterre town council, a meeting that will be attended by the federal and provincial Members for Abitibi East, Rouyn-Noranda, Abitibi West and Ungava, and by the Abitibi-Temiscamingue regional development committee for railway transportation.

subtopic: ANNOUNCED SHUTDOWN OF PRINCE RUPERT STATION CFPR
ANNOUNCED SHUTDOWN OF PRINCE RUPERT STATION CFPR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while the Minister of Communications (Miss MacDonald) undertakes the extraordinary step of having Cabinet review Allarcom's allnews channel bid, and Canmet's entry into the telephone market, CBC Radio is shutting down its award winning station CFPR-Prince Rupert and the Minister refuses to do anything.
According to the recent Task Force on Broadcasting Policy, the per capita cost of providing local news coverage to all under-serviced areas in Canada amounts to a mere 10 cents per year. The Mulroney Government has hacked and slashed the CBC budget to the point where, in order for the good people of the British Columbia interior to receive improvements in CBC Radio, another region of British Columbia, the northwest, must suffer.
The Broadcasting Act of Canada states that CBC must serve "the special needs of geographic regions". Surely closing CFPR in Prince Rupert, and reducing local northwest B.C. reporting to ad hoc broadcasts through Prince George, violate the intent of the Act and the intent of Parliament.
The B.C. northwest and the B.C. northeast are distinct geographic regions. They can both be served more effectively by CBC, and while I will be putting pressure on the corporation to stop plans to shut down CFPR, I also call upon the Minister of Communications to display a commitment to extending public broadcasting. If resources are to be slashed to the CBC it in turn cannot meet its legislated responsibility to the people of B.C.
1 urge the Minister of Communications to wake up and realize what her Government's continued attacks upon public broadcasting mean to the people who live in the regions of Canada.

subtopic: DIFFICULTY IN ATTRACTING SKILLED MINING PERSONNEL
DIFFICULTY IN ATTRACTING SKILLED MINING PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, mining narrow veins calls for a high degree of skill and judgment on the part of the individual miner. Until the recent

February 12, 1988
gold boom Canada had concentrated on large scale mining so now we have a shortage of conventional miners. Recently Cornish miners have had to be imported into Nova Scotia. In my riding, mine managers tell me of their great difficulty in attracting skilled personnel.
High wages are now being offered in the mines, and I would encourage young people to look to a career in this industry.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard), recognizing the problem, has designated "hard rock miner" as a "shortage occupation" and, as such, eligible for training assistance under the Skills Shortages Program. This will certainly help.

Mr. Speaker, they say the best speech is a short speech. Bearing that in mind, I think the time has come for the Government of Canada to declare that Montreal is "spatial". Enough of this shillyshallying and procrastination. Montreal is not special but spatial.

Montreal is not special but "spatial".
Bravo!
A Conservative says "Bravo"!

subtopic: CHARTERED BANKS-FUNDING OF FOREIGN LOAN LOSSES- INVESTIGATION SUGGESTED
CHARTERED BANKS-FUNDING OF FOREIGN LOAN LOSSES- INVESTIGATION SUGGESTED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, preliminary analysis of the 1987 profits in Canada of major banks and trust companies indicates that the profit per hundred dollars of Canadian assets administered reached alltime highs, some 35 per cent greater than the previous record.
All Canadians know that our chartered banks experienced massive losses on foreign loans in 1987. However, none cut dividends, unlike in the United States where the big money centre banks still face strong regional competition.
The finance committee and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre) should consider an investigation under the Competition Act to see whether large Canadian banks are acting together to fund their foreign loan losses on the backs of Canadian consumers.

subtopic: OPENING OF GAMES IN CALGARY-GOOD WISHES TO ATHLETES-GRATITUDE TO ORGANIZERS
OPENING OF GAMES IN CALGARY-GOOD WISHES TO ATHLETES-GRATITUDE TO ORGANIZERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have reason to be proud today, because tomorrow the Winter Olympics open in Calgary. After months of careful preparation, the big day has come at last. The world's best athletes are now in Alberta, and we wish them all the best of luck.
To all those in Calgary who worked so hard to organize this international event, we say: Thank you!

I want to take a few moments to mention the many thousands of other ordinary people who rarely get recognized at a time like this, and whose dedication has allowed these athletes to excel. I refer to the coaches who labour long and hard, often early in the morning or late at night, especially the minor league coaches who help to teach the basic skills and transform our children into future champions; to the parents who sacrifice so much, and who underwrite so much of the cost of developing the skills our athletes need to challenge the world; and to the thousands of others who organize the leagues, run the track meets, and provide the infrastructure we all need.
All of those people have contributed to the Olympic Games. They are their games, and they should be truly proud of them. Once again, best wishes to our athletes who, we know, will represent us and themselves to the best of their abilities. They are truly champions in our hearts.

subtopic: SINKING OF OCEAN RANGER OIL DRILLING RIG-ROYAL COMMISSION'S RECOMMENDATIONS

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
subtopic: SINKING OF OCEAN RANGER OIL DRILLING RIG-ROYAL COMMISSION'S RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Monday, February 15, 1988 will mark the sixth anniversary of the sinking of the Ocean Ranger in the wintry Atlantic off the east coast of Newfoundland. On that evening 84 men lost their lives.
The Royal Commission into this tragedy noted that "the loss of the Ocean Ranger was caused by a chain of events which resulted from a coincidence of severe storm conditions, design inadequacy and lack of knowledgeable human intervention". The Royal Commission produced 136 recommendations aimed at preventing a similar tragedy. The federal Government and oil companies have quickly acted on quite a number of those recommendations, but many remain ignored to this point.
Today, six years after the sinking of the Ocean Ranger, individuals who work on drilling rigs off eastern Canada are
February 12, 1988

still at terrible risk if they must abandon the rigs and take to the sea in storm conditions.
John Parsons, an engineer hired by the Newfoundland Government to examine safety in offshore drilling, has stated that the existing lifeboat escape systems remain appallingly inadequate. Mr. Parsons has suggested that an independent safety division be created with wide powers of enforcement within the Canada-Newfoundland Offshore Petroleum Board to minimize conflicts between the drive for energy selfsufficiency and the need for safety for people working on the rigs.
As bad as the Ocean Ranger disaster was some six years ago with the loss of 84 lives, what would be worse is if we failed to heed the advice and the lessons that we should have learned six years ago at the cost of 84 lives, and at a cost of $15 million for a Royal Commission to make recommendations to ensure that those who work in the harsh wintry conditions of the Atlantic, and elsewhere in offshore rigs, are safe, and that we have done everything humanly possible to protect them.

Second, continuity and a fair corporate income tax system. We have delivered. Third, keeping interest rates under control, and we delivered on that as well. subtopic: BLACK HISTORY MONTH-TRIBUTE TO OUTSTANDING ACHIEVERS
BLACK HISTORY MONTH-TRIBUTE TO OUTSTANDING ACHIEVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, February is Black History Month, a worth-while time to reflect upon the magnificent contribution to our nation of Canadians descended from the nations of Africa.
Great black Canadians of the past include Matthew da Costa, who arrived in Canada with Champlain in 1605; William Hall of Nova Scotia who was the first Canadian to win the Victoria Cross; Mary Ann Shadd, lawyer, teacher, fiery editor, and abolitionist in 19th Century Upper Canada; Portia White, the great opera singer; and Delos Davis, the first black King's Counsel in the British Empire.
These giants paved the way for those who excel today: Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario and former Member of Parliament Lincoln Alexander, author Austin Clarke, jazz pianist Oscar Peterson, Order of Canada recipients Carrie Best, William P. Oliver, and Alton Parker; Juno Award winners Dan Hill, Lillian Allen, and Billy Newton-Davis; the fastest man alive, Ben Johnson; one of the fastest women alive, Angela Issajenko; and such leaders as provincial ombudsmen Daniel Hill, Gordon Earle, former Nova Scotia Human Rights Commissioner George McCurdy, and former British Columbia MLA Rosemary Brown.
The list of achievers is endless and bears witness to the historic mission of black Canadians to strive for the attainment of the highest democratic ideals-liberty, justice, and equality-despite the obstacles of discrimination and bigotry that sadly exist. Yet, this month reminds us that, no matter how long the struggle, they have overcome.
Of course I want to add to the list the Hon. Member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy).

subtopic: BLACK HISTORY MONTH-TRIBUTE TO OUTSTANDING ACHIEVERS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: HAMILTON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT-INTRODUCTION OF DAILY FLIGHTS TO JOHN F. KENNEDY AIRPORT
HAMILTON INTERNATIONAL AIRPORT-INTRODUCTION OF DAILY FLIGHTS TO JOHN F. KENNEDY AIRPORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to report that, after months of working and waiting, Air Crosby Control has given us a final clearance and Hamilton's International Airport is about to take off.
The approval of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) today for Pan Am Express to operate three flights a day to John F. Kennedy Airport from Hamilton potentially makes our airport one of the great airports in the country.

February 12, 1988
It is a major and welcome initiative by the Mulroney Government to help relieve the congestion at Toronto International Airport.
I am delighted to have received the assistance of political representatives from four levels of government and all three Parties in our area in convincing Transport Canada to give this much needed vote of confidence to Hamilton's airport. The Hon. Members for Niagara Falls, Hamilton West, St. Catharines, Brant, Haldimand-Norfolk, Erie, Welland, Lincoln, Burlington, Halton and even Hamilton Mountain and Hamilton East, and many others helped.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that we are not supposed to mention Members by name, but I will say: ''Bless you, John Crosbie; thank you, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney".

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is here, because as we reflect upon the effects of the Mulroney-Wilson Budget and tax reform package, I would like to remember the words of Frank Scott who once wrote:
Low income individuals and families pay a higher proportion of their incomes in all kinds of taxes than those with higher incomes.
The poem was entitled Cent ans d'injustice and was written in 1967. Some 21 years later we can only add:
[ Translation]
The more it changes, the more it is the same.

[English)

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Government of Ontario and its so-called saviour has abdicated a major responsibility to the municipalities- Sunday shopping. What a cowardly, shameful decision on behalf of the people of Ontario.
The Supreme Court of Canada has said that Ontario has the authority to legislate Sunday closings, and Ontario has refused. That is not leadership. That is a cop-out.
Church leaders, business leaders, politicians, and ordinary Ontarians are banding together to form the Coalition Against Opening Sunday Shopping. The Ottawa-Carleton Board of Trade Chairman, Tim Whitehead, and its President, Lisa
Hopkins, have sent a clear message of opposition to Queen's Park. They have all got my vote. This is an outrageous decision.

Mr. Speaker, the National Action Committee on the Status of Women has recently written to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) saying that in light of the new spirit of co-operation between the U.S.S.R. and the U.S.A., it is asking him to withdraw the Department of Defence White Paper. It says:
Instead of re-affirming our differences with the Soviet Union, escalating further the very dangerous arms race, and increasing our economic military burden, we are asking you to adopt a more rational, humane, and effective policy.
Already, we can see a decline in government services as people live on the streets and line up for food. As the accompanying chart shows, far more jobs are created in responding to human needs in Canada and around the world than in military production. We also do not believe that more weapons make us more secure. We prefer non-provocative defence and nuclear free areas, particularly a nuclear free Arctic verified by all the Arctic nations.
The deployment of expensive nuclear-powered submarines we believe endangers the fragile ecosystem and violates the spirit if not the letter of the Non-Proliferation Treaty. The cost of one submarine could radically improve life for the one million Canadian children who live below the poverty line.

subtopic: RESPONSIBLE MANAGEMENT OF GOVERNMENT FINANCES- REDUCTION OF DEFICIT
RESPONSIBLE MANAGEMENT OF GOVERNMENT FINANCES- REDUCTION OF DEFICIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, nothing is more basic to a strong framework for private sector growth and job creation than responsible management of government finances.
In 1984 the federal deficit and national debt were almost out of control. The Government's first priority had to be to get government spending under control. We have done so.
This week's Budget maintains the course of consistent adherence to fiscal principles first set out in November, 1984. We are achieving the fiscal targets we set ourselves. We are achieving steady year to year declines in the deficit. The reduction projected for 1988-89 will be the first time in the post-war period that the deficit has declined four years in a row.
Canada's strong economic growth, coupled with the Government's fiscal program, has created the capacity to carry forward the Government's commitment to priority programs.
February 12, 1988

The Government is committed to ensuring an economic future that provides challenging opportunities for our children and economic security for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance is probably aware that, while his high interest rate policy might suit Central Canada, it is extremely harmful for the remote regions, where the major problem is not inflation, but unemployment. Yesterday, the chief economist of the research firm Data Resources joined the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Canadian Manufacturers' Association in asking for lower interest rates.
Here is what I want to ask the Minister of Finance: Does he intend to resume his discussions with the Governor of the Bank of Canada to try to convince him that the current interest rate policy is not necessary and that it affects mostly the remote regions of Canada and is especially harmful to the unemployed in those regions?

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 think 1 have responded on a number of occasions to that particular question. What I should say to the Hon. Member is that interest rates are down 3 percentage points from what they were when we came into office. They are down about one and a quarter to one and a half per cent from what they were in October of last year. The bank rate came down an eighth of 1 per cent yesterday.
In response to the Hon. Member's concerns about the regions of the country, let me say to him that we must have one monetary policy for the whole of the country, but fiscal policy can be addressed directly to particular regions.
Let me just read what we have done for Newfoundland, to pick one province. The transportation and highways ERDA agreement, $112 million; the pulp and paper ERDA agreement, $38 million; forestry resource development, $33 million; Channel of Port aux Basques water supply, $6.5 million; Newfoundland offshore development fund, $225 million; Goose Bay airport redevelopment, $93 million; the FBI equity injection of $77 million; Terra Transport and other transportation-I could go on and on, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF INTEREST RATE POLICY
speechtext: The Hon. Minister of Finance says that he could go on and on. I have no doubt that he would have.

subtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT RATE IN CERTAIN REGIONS- GOVERNMENT STRATEGY TO HELP WORKERS
HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT RATE IN CERTAIN REGIONS- GOVERNMENT STRATEGY TO HELP WORKERS
speechtext:

February 12, 1988

what he said, that unemployment in Newfoundland is still three times as high as in Central Canada. The same is true in the Gaspe and several other regions. subtopic: HIGH UNEMPLOYMENT RATE IN CERTAIN REGIONS- GOVERNMENT STRATEGY TO HELP WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member had not prepared that question before the House sat, he probably would not have asked it because 1 answered that question as part of my responses to his first and second questions.
1 should point out to the Hon. Member that the unemployment rate is down in every province of the country compared to the rate this time last year. That is very real progress. It is down in every province of Canada, with the exception of Prince Edward Island where it is marginally up since we came into office in September of 1984.
Again, there has been very clear progress. As I have indicated to the Hon. Member on many occasions in the past, we have generated an over-all economic policy which has resulted in Canada being first in economic growth, first in employment growth and first in productivity performance of the major industrialized countries. Because we have that growth and that economic performance, we have been able to provide the resources through the Atlantic Opportunities Agency, the equalization programs, the Atlantic enterprise purchasing program, the Newfoundland Development Accord and the various highways agreements. subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- COMPLIANCE BY MANITOBA PROVINCE
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- COMPLIANCE BY MANITOBA PROVINCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Deputy Prime Minister. On Wednesday I asked the Prime Minister a question concerning the U.S. administration's threat to demand compensation or redress if there was not full compliance by the provinces with the continental trade program. Today we have word that the Province of Manitoba will now introduce legislation that will void parts of the agreement, and the Province of Ontario is prepared to do the same.
The Government cannot duck the question any longer. The Government has put itself in a constitutional box between the provinces and the U.S. administration. It is heading toward a constitutional crisis. The Government must take a position on this matter and Parliament deserves an answer.
What is the Government going to do? How is it going to respond to the U.S. administration's demand that it pay compensation if provinces do not comply, because those provinces have no intention of complying?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Treasury Board; Minister responsible for Privatization and Regulatory Affairs; Vice-President; President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT- COMPLIANCE BY MANITOBA PROVINCE

Mr. Speaker, I think the Prime Minister dealt with that question quite fully. As far as the current issue he has raised is concerned, I want to remind the Hon. Member, as he knows, that never before in the history of an international treaty has there been so much consultation and dialogue between the two levels of government. Right from the very beginning this issue was the subject of numerous First Ministers' Conferences and bilateral meetings. Member should know very well that since the free trade arrangement will be good for all regions of the country and good for all the provinces, rather than joining forces with the provinces which are expressing reluctance with certain elements of it, he should show some leadership at the national level and should encourage all provinces to become party to this agreement. He should do that rather than getting on the bandwagon trying to destroy what is a good agreement for all Canadians and a good agreement for every region of the country.

Mr. Speaker, that kind of answer simply will not wash any more. The fact is that the Government has put this country in a position of being subject to major intimidation by the United States administration which is demanding compensation or redress. In other words, the Americans will up the ante on the agreement. Several provinces say that they cannot go along with this and, while there may have been consultations, there was no approval.
When will the Government clearly spell out how it intends to deal with the dilemma it finds itself in with the constitutional crisis we are heading for and the major revisions of the agreement that will be required by the Americans under the circumstances if there is no provincial compliance? That is a very serious question and it deserves a proper answer, not the kind of ducking and weaving we have had so far.

premiums, the payroll tax, the income tax and all those other unpopular measures the NDP Government of Manitoba is engaged in. If you're with them, join them!

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have a question for the Minister of Finance about fairness in taxation. The Minister has acknowledged that some 60,000 profitable Canadian corporations will pay no federal tax this year after his tax reform.
Is he aware that in 1986 companies like Hees International with profits of $170 million, Brascan with profits of $187 million, and Alcan Aluminum with profits of $220 million, paid no corporate tax? Is he aware that in 1987 companies like Cadillac-Fairview with profits of $95 million and Bramalea with profits of $51 million paid no federal corporate tax?
Why will companies like this continue to get a free ride after 1988? Why will the Minister not bring a minimum corporate tax into force?

subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT MINIMUM CORPORATE TAX BE INTRODUCED
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is on the finance committee, and he is well aware that corporate tax reform addresses many of these problems which resulted in profitable companies not paying income tax. That is being dealt with in stage one of tax reform and I know the Hon. Member is going to give us his full support to get that tax reform provision through. The result will be that $5 billion in additional taxes will be paid by corporations over the next five years.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the same Minister.
The Minister says his tax reform will increase corporate tax revenue. Does he realize that in the United States, tax reform has resulted in an increase in corporate tax revenue which, in relative terms, is twice the increase we will see in Canada, and that this is largely due to the fact that the United States has a minimum corporate tax?
Why is the Government reluctant to introduce a minimum corporate tax in Canada, which would introduce additional revenue that could be used in new measures to create jobs and eliminate regional disparity in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, let me give the Hon. Member some examples of the type of company that would be caught by the type of minimum tax he is proposing.

Member is quite aware suffers from high levels of unemployment. subtopic: STATISTICS CANADA REPORT-EFFECTIVE RATE OF CORPORATE TAX
STATISTICS CANADA REPORT-EFFECTIVE RATE OF CORPORATE TAX

aid solution as he is proposing. We have caused a change in the nature of the corporate tax system that will deal with it in a fundamental way. That is surely the right way to deal with the matter.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TRANSPORT OF PLUTONIUM OVER NORTHERN CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 have the honour and duty under Standing Order 106 to present petitions signed by 150 residents of Eskimo Point, Rankin Inlet, Spence Bay, and Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories.
The petitioners are concerned about the possible detrimental environmental effects and the contribution to nuclear proliferation that might be occasioned by flying plutonium over northern Canadian territory as is proposed in the U.S.-Japan agreement.
Therefore, the petitioners pray and call upon the Parliament of Canada to recognize the dangers of such flights and to say no to the transport of plutonium over northern Canadian territory.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege and responsibility to present a petition duly certified.
It is from a number of Canadians who point out that the very fabric of Canadian sovereignty is threatened by the proposed Mulroney-Reagan trade deal, that the Government has no mandate to negotiate a deal, such as this with the United States, that the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal would reduce Canada's ability to plan the economic, social and cultural programs that we need, and that the deal would integrate Canada further into the North American defence industrial base.
Therefore, they ask the House of Commons to ensure that a national debate take place on the trade deal and that this debate results in a national general election before the agreement is finalized.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED FREE TRADE
speechtext:
I have a petition duly certified by the Clerk of Petitions. It is from Canadians living in Toronto and in Halifax.
They are concerned with the trade deal negotiated by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with the President of the United States because the Prime Minister had no mandate for that deal. It also fails to secure for Canadians access to the U.S. market which was the key objective in the stated negotiations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Yukon (Ms. McLaughlin) has the floor.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to continue my comments on Bill C-109. Before Question Period I was discussing the idea that the necessity for such a large borrowing Bill would not have arisen if there were some indication in the Minister's Budget that there would be innovative measures to deal with regional disparity. For example, the Minister did not mention in his Budget speech that the Government has cut back $3 billion in regional development since 1984.
Looking at the current Budget from the perspective of regional development, which I am interested in because of the area 1 represent, it indicates that there will be $3 million cut in non-statutory programs. It is not defined in the Budget just exactly what these non-statutory programs will be. The nonstatutory programs deal with the operation costs of federal Government subsidies to industry, payments to Crown corporations, capital spending, grants and contributions. This leaves the field wide open as to where the Government might decide to make these cuts.
My concern is that because we do not have the Estimates and we do not have any specifics about where these cuts will be. certain areas of the country, in particular the regions to the east, the north and the west which are most vulnerable, could be seriously affected by these cuts in non-statutory programs. Vulnerable is defined as those with the least votes in this instance.
As an example I mention a particular program in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories that has led to increased economic activity there. I refer to the economic development agreement with such sub-agreements as the one that deals with tourism. This has helped the small lodge owner to increase and to develop their businesses. It has enabled them to do some advertising to bring in the tourist dollars. This is but one example of the economic development agreement. These are non-statutory programs and it is therefore of great concern to us that these not be programs from which the Government will choose to cut. I refer to programs which stimulate investment in development in the more isolated regions of the country. These are vulnerable programs and give us great concern. They are the ones easiest to cut because of the fewer number of voters.
February 12, 1988

I would also point to programs oriented to the aboriginal people, the Native Economic Development Program and the special ERDA which have helped people in those aboriginal communities to develop small business and become selfsufficient, which should be an objective of all of us. We will be looking closely to see if the cuts in the non-statutory programs do in fact increase regional disparity, which is a very important issue for all of us across Canada.
I mentioned earlier in my remarks that it is my view and my Party's view that in presenting this Budget there were places where the Government could have looked to raise revenues. We have heard much about the increase in the corporate tax, and the corporations that do not pay taxes. One area where the Government systematically looks to raise revenues is from the pocket of the ordinary taxpayer. The Government has projected that this will be done again with the one cent increase on gasoline. This seems to be a repetitive theme, and that is part of the problem with this Budget and why under this borrowing Bill we are asked to approve such a large sum. All of the ideas of the Government are repetitive; there is nothing innovative or new.
For example, there was an increase in the tax on fuel in November, 1984 which amounted to almost 10 cents a gallon at the pumps. In the May, 1985 Budget there was an increase of two cents per litre or nine cents per gallon at the pumps. On June 27, 1985 there was another increase of one cent per litre on gasoline. In February, 1987 there was another one cent per litre increase, and in February, 1988 another one cent per litre. It seems to me that the Government is in a rut, and there must be other ways that I will suggest where that money could be raised.
I wish to say a few words about how this one cent per litre on gasoline affects the more isolated regions, regions like my own, the Yukon, the Northwest Territories, northern parts of the provinces, and the Atlantic provinces. That is where this type of tax hurts.
For example, in the far north our costs are very high. Our cost of living is anywhere from 30 to 50 per cent above that of Edmonton. An increase in fuel prices, even excluding diesel fuel, which I understand is excluded, really affects small business, or the person who has to make deliveries around the territory, where he or she may travel 1,000 miles to make a delivery. It is a serious problem for us. Every increase like this to the cost of living for the northerner is an exponential increase compared to that for people who live south of 60. It is still tough on them, but for us it is doubly tough.
Another aspect of the fuel tax is the thinking behind which the Government decides to raise revenue. Perhaps, as much as anything, this sums up the philosophy of the Government, and it is something that Canadians taxpayers will want to take note of. This one cent per litre tax will apply to aviation gasoline for propeller aircraft, for example, the Twin Otter, and the small aircraft used by bush pilots and charter companies, not only in
Borrowing Authority
the North, but in many small areas throughout Canada. However, the tax will not apply to jet fuel. Everyone knows that the revenues that could have been raised from jet fuel would be far in excess of those raised from taxing the small one or two person business or the small airline. This is an example of how the Government once again wants to hit the little guy, but it is hands off the jet set.
Northerners and those who live in more isolated areas are much more severely affected by these measures, for example, a simple thing in one sense like one cent on a litre of gasoline, will have very serious affects for a number of families and small businesses.
Another example of how the Government might have looked at some innovative measures that would reduce the need for the $23.5 billion that we are asked to approve on this borrowing Bill is to look at its priorities and its development.
In the Yukon the Alaska Highway is our one vital and key link for transportation, investment, and development. If that highway is not in a reasonable condition, and we are not asking for a four lane highway but a reasonable highway that can be travelled, our tourism and our ability to attract investment are significantly impacted. What is this Government's priority? It is to cut the budget by 50 per cent for this highway, our one link to the outside.
We heard the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) say, "If you want to develop constitutionally, become self-sufficient". We are being told to become self-sufficient at the same time as funds are being cut which would have helped us to increase our self-sufficiency. It does not make sense, and that seems to be the thrust of much of this Budget.
The other area I wish to mention is what I referred to as the peekaboo sales tax philosophy of the Government. In the Budget report the Government talks about future reforms of sales tax. Anyone can read between the lines on that one. Between the lines it says, After the election, we will tell you what will happen. We have already felt the effects of the 10 per cent increase in the telecommunications tax. That again hits the isolated regions and the people who have to maintain contact with southern Canada for professional, business and family reasons, particularly in the riding that I represent. How does this help development? How does this help to raise revenues in order that we do not have to borrow as much as we do at this time?
I do not want to appear ungrateful, because I did note in the Budget that there was a removal of duties on model glider kits and burial shrouds. That will benefit northerners as well as other Canadians, and we are certainly pleased that this innovative measure has been taken at this time.
The introduction of the northern allowance was another way that the Government could have redressed some of the disparities that I have mentioned.

February 12, 1988
Borrowing Authority
If the Government had made this a tax credit rather than a tax allowance, lower income and lower middle income people would have benefited to the same degree as higher income people. Certainly, it is a good measure, and I am not criticizing the measure, but it is a half measure. If it could have been made a deduction more people would have benefited, more people who now pay very high housing costs would benefit. But again it is only directed to those with higher incomes. The people with lower incomes have the toughest time raising their families in the North.
What about the other innovative measures that we have seen from the Government on raising revenues? Since the Government took office in 1984 personal income taxes have gone up a whopping 38 per cent, while the tax paid by corporations has increased only by 28 per cent. This leads me to one of the glaring inequities of the Government's philosophy of raising revenues.
We know that there are 60,000 profit making companies which still pay no tax. Last year there were more than 500 Canadians listed as making more than $200,000 a year who paid no tax. This is not very much comfort to the single parent who is raising two children, for example, on earnings at about the poverty line, somewhere slightly under $20,000, and has found her taxes going up each year from 1985 to 1987. Total taxes dropped from about $1,800 in 1987 to $1,355 in 1988 thanks to tax reform. However, the 1988 amount is still higher than the tax bill paid by that same single parent of $1,200 in
1984.	It will be very difficult to explain to that person how the Budget will help her and that there is sound rationale for the amount of borrowing we must do at this time.
As we have said before, a minimum corporate tax would certainly have served to address some of these issues and to raise revenues in a fair manner and consistent with what we in the New Democratic Party feel, that is, that the burden of taxation should be spread across society, not just applied to the average person who is trying to raise his or her family. Each time a new Budget comes out, we see that that is who has been hit.
I should like to refer to one comment in The Budget Speech of the Minister which I think is quite important. It reflects on the amount of money that he is seeking approval to borrow. The revenues projected in the Minister's Budget are based on a very optimistic and rosy view of the economy. The Government says that in 1989 the rate of economic growth is expected to rebound with consumer expenditures buoyed by refunds from tax reform. I have just mentioned the situation of a single parent. It may be that the shareholders of companies that do not pay taxes will be out buying a bit more. It is a very hopeful scenario and, as a Canadian, I hope it comes true. However, we must look at what is realistic. It appears from the Government's figures, as I mentioned earlier, that there will be reductions in unemployment insurance contributions. We can expect more unemployment and reduced incomes. If they are
making and contributing less, how can they possibly consume more?
The Canadian Manufacturers' Association and other investment counsellors have a less optimistic outlook for 1989. We hope that they are wrong, but perhaps they are looking at the Government's own figures and predicting more unemployment than the Government wishes to predict. Obviously many hopes and dreams are built into the Budget, and we will see what will happen.
I want to support my Party's point about minimum tax for corporations. What the Budget shows is that we must look at how to realign our spending priorities and our revenue raising priorities. There is a possibility to do that. It is not something that is pie in the sky; it can be done. We have certainly made a number of suggestions in that regard.
In summary, I want to refer to what is in the Budget for different groups, for example, women and families. There are increased travel costs. We see that money has been put into regressive tax measures which do not help average families who need child care. We do not see increased child care spaces so that those members of families who want to work know that while they are working their families are in safe, quality child care, and that the children of the future receive the break they need. We do not see anything in the Budget for these people.
1 would also like to refer to what is not in the Budget for aboriginal people. We know that the first nations have many problems such as poor housing. They have a need for economic development, a need to receive assistance to establish a good economic base, and a need for social programs. We do not see any recognizable, targeted measures for aboriginal peoples.
What about the North? The North is only mentioned once in the Budget in reference to the northern allowance being excluded from the tax preferences which are subject to minimum tax. Certainly that measure is consistent with the principle of recognizing the extra financial burden of living in the North, but in fact it will only affect those with incomes of over $50,000. It will not affect the average northerner or the average single parent who is trying to pay for child care. Some men and women are looking for and want jobs. They do not want part-time or temporary ones. They want full-time jobs that are meaningful so that they can contribute to Canadian society, which will raise tax revenues and help decrease the amount of money it would be necessary to borrow.
Surely the deficit is of concern to every Canadian. However, I am suggesting that a rethinking of priorities is needed. We must all work toward reducing the deficit, but corporations and taxpayers alike should share the burden. At the moment individual taxpayers are carrying an unfair share of the burden. All the Budget does is underscore that with a one cent tax on fuel and a decrease in certain programs.
Do we really need to spend billions of dollars on nuclear submarines? It seems to me that that is a very good question. Often child care people and defence people are fighting it out
February 12, 1988

for the money. Spending on nuclear submarines, which fortunately the Government has said it will not use for any offensive purpose, is a very skewed priority and does not contribute in a meaningful way to our economy, to the North where many of these submarines would be located, or to reducing the deficit about which we are all worried.
Perhaps the Budget was designed to do nothing. In some ways it meets that criterion. Some people have called it a preelection Budget. I guess it was a pre-election tranquilizer so that we would not notice some of the more serious ramifications of the philosophy behind the Budget. Once again they will make sure that the little guy pays. They are not going to tax jet fuel. No, they will not touch the jet setters, but they will touch the small guy or the small business. On reflection, the Minister has not really presented us with a "do-nothing" Budget, in that it is an indication of the Government's philosophy and priorities with which my Party and I have great difficulty agreeing. We do not feel that it addresses the major outstanding issues in Canada today.
On that note I should like to conclude by saying that Bill C-109 under discussion today is simply a reflection of the state we are in, the necessity to approve the borrowing of a large amount of money without knowing-we do not have the Estimates-exactly to what it is said to be directed and without knowing who will be vulnerable to the proposed cuts in the Budget.
The Government must take a serious look at its priorities. I can assure its Members that in the next election Canadians will be watching very carefully.
