subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1988-89 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to comment on Bill C-109, legislation that, if passed, will allow the Government to increase the national debt by $25.3 billion during the financial year starting April 1.
Mr. Speaker, the charge on a loan of $25.3 billion, if calculated according to the medium and long-term interest rates in effect today, will cost over the next financial year, and 1 am referring to 1989-90, a total of $2.5 billion. If interest rates continue to rise, this may well entail additional expenditures that will spread to future budgets.
Mr. Speaker, at the end of this financial year, Canada's national debt will have reached nearly $300 billion. Nobody has ever had that much money in his bank account, let alone his billfold. This is a lot of money, a little over $12,000 per Canadian man, woman and child. This money is largely owed to other Canadians, but nevertheless, the federal Government has to pay a certain amount of money annually just to pay the interest on the national debt, and these annual expenditures are now as high as $30 billion per year. This means that every Canadian man, woman and child would have to pay an
Borrowing Authority
average of a little over $1,000 per year in taxes just to pay the interest on the national debt. Obviously, when we realize that children, for instance, and some people who may or may not be in the labour force do not pay income tax, this is an enormous burden.
Mr. Speaker, on the Government side there is a tendency to say that the deficit and the debt we have today were created by the previous Government.
1 would like to take a few moments to argue this point. The Conservatives are saying: "When you Liberals were in power, you had deficits, and now we are trying to deal with them". I may remind the Conservative Government that although we had quite substantial deficits in 1981, 1982, and 1983, it was because the world economy, so not just Canada but the entire Western world, was in an economic recession. It was the worst recession since the Great Depression in the thirties.
1 hear businessmen, merchants say: "Deficits are always bad". Here is my usual question to those business people: What would you have done in 1982, 1983, 1984, when the recession caused high unemployment, what would you have done had the Government decided, in order to avoid any deficit, to cut most social programs, unemployment insurance, etc? Clearly, the first victims would have been people in need, but the second victims would have been merchants, businessmen, industries producing the goods that were bought by people who, even though they were depending on unemployment insurance or welfare thanks to that State intervention, had the financial resources to buy some consumer goods, which allowed a hurting economy to go through that period. Now, and this is what I am blaming the Conservatives for, if it is acceptable to accumulate deficits in times of economic depression and large unemployment in order to help unemployed workers survive a difficult period, this had practically no justification any more once economic renewal ensured that the rate of growth of the economy had gone up, and especially when after six years of economic growth, we found ourselves in a situation that is just as bad and even a lot worse than the 1981, 1982 and early 1983 recession.
Mr. Speaker, looking at the figures, we see that this Conservative Government promised wonders but did not deliver. Let me recall that during the elections, the Conservative Party made a lot of promises. Maybe two or three people referred to the deficit, but one of them, the Leader of the Liberal Party of Canada, Mr. Turner, raised the problem during the election because he knew the depression was improving, renewal had started since the middle of 1983 and this concern had to be addressed if we were to get out of the depression. But the Conservatives promised wonders. What did they promise for instance?
I shall now read what the Conservatives had promised. 1 have quoted this a number of times, but as the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) seems to indicate that I am quoting out of context, I went back to Hansard, and instead of reading only one sentence, 1 shall now read an entire paragraph to

February 12, 1988
Borrowing Authority
show that the Conservative Party had made very firm commitments to the Canadian people when in Opposition.
The population believed the promise made by the present Minister of Finance, who was then a member of the Opposition representing the Etobicoke Centre riding. On March 6, 1984, the Elon. Member for Etobicoke Centre stated what follows in this very Elouse, and he may even have been sitting in the seat I now occupy myself.
I shall quote him in English, as the text I have before me is in English.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was in Opposition and made a speech about the Budget, he asked himself questions and answered his own questions. Fie said:
Then the question is: How would you cut; would you cut by raising taxes or by cutting government spending? Again the answer is very clear. We would cut spending. We would not raise taxes. Tax levels in Canada are already too high. Spending cuts are important for another reason. If we raise taxes, we provide more funds for politicians and bureaucrats to spend.
Can you imagine that, Mr. Speaker? When the Minister of Finance was in Opposition, not only did he say that a Tory Government would not increase taxes but he said that the reason for that was that the taxes were too high. I think I agree with him about that. He also said that raising taxes would give more money for politicians and civil servants to spend.
After three and a half years of this Tory Government, can we say that the Minister of Finance and all the Tory backbenchers who repeated his words during the election campaign lived up to their promises? Certainly not.
I have said on other occasions and will repeat once again, because it is so important in this debate, that this is a question of credibility. Can we trust this Government? Can we trust this Minister of Finance? He said in 1984, a few months before the election, that he would not raise taxes and that he would cut expenses. That was a commitment he made on behalf of his Party. Probably many Canadians thought that his Party was serious.
After three and a half years of administration by a Party which said it would not increase taxes, here is the list, not an exhaustive list but just a few examples, of the broken promises. Those broken promises go to the heart of the question of credibility. Can we trust this Party if it now says that it will not increase taxes in the future? Can we believe it? Are we prepared to vote for this Party? When this Party says it will cut the deficit completely or will reduce it to the level of $20 billion, can we trust it now? It lied to us in the past. I believe that when it does that once, it can do it again.
Here is the list of the new taxes imposed by this Government which said that it would never increase taxes to cut the deficit. Soon after it was elected, on October 1, it increased the federal
sales tax by 1 per cent, from 9 per cent to 10 per cent. On January 1, 1986 it increased the manufacturers' sales tax by another percentage point to 11 per cent. On April 1, 1986, there was another increase of 1 per cent to 12 per cent. That is three increases in less than two years in the manufacturers' sales tax.
This Government which said it would never increase taxes increased the manufacturers' sales tax by 3 per cent and now more companies have to pay sales taxes, thus increasing prices to the consumers. The first extension to it was on July 1, 1985, and the second on July 1, 1987, for an additional half a billion dollars.
The sales tax increased from 8 per cent to 12 per cent on paint, wallpaper and toys on January 1, 1988. There was an increase in the gasoline tax, and the Minister deserves the gold medal for the gasoline tax.
The Tories say that when the Liberals were in power they increased taxes on gasoline. 1 ask the Tories, do they know why? It was part of a policy to Canadianize companies in the oil and gas industry, to make sure Canadians owned the resource, not foreigners. It was to make sure Canadians manage their own economy and to be both les locataires et les proprietaires. We had a policy to make sure Canadians own their resources but the Government cancelled that policy and retained the tax on gasoline. Not only that, it increased the tax to an almost unbearable level.
On September 3, 1985, that Government and that Minister put in place a two cent per litre tax on gasoline and diesel fuel. They added another cent on January 1, 1987. Another cent in February, 1987. Can you imagine, 4 cents in a very short period of time. A few days ago they added another cent to reach 5 cents per litre. Translate that into a gallon. A lot of Canadians are more aware of the Imperial system than the metric system. People my age understand the gallon but have difficulty with the litre. My children have no problem but I am getting old and I have a problem; that is why I want to translate it into gallons. Five cents per litre is 23 cents per gallon. When we take into consideration the 3 per cent increase in sales taxes, it adds up to 27 cents per gallon.
Can you imagine, in three and a half years that Party which said publicly it would help the resource industry, help the gas and oil producer, has increased the price of gasoline by 27 cents a gallon. I was not a Member of this Parliament in 1979 when the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) tabled a Budget on behalf of the Tory Government which included a tax increase of 18 cents a gallon tax. The Government was defeated on that increase. If a Tory Government was defeated over an 18-cent tax increase, can you imagine what will happen with 27 cents?
That is not the end of the broken promises. That Minister, who said on March 6, 1984 that he would not increase taxes, has increased taxes on tobacco on four different occasions: the
February 12, 1988

first was on May 24, 1985, for S340 million, the second was on February 27, 1986, for $150 million, the third was on February 19, 1986, for $75 million, and the fourth was on January 1, 1988, for $175 million. For a Minister who said he would not increase taxes, that is quite a record.
That is only on the consumer side, though there are a few others. After having increased sales taxes, enlarged the base of the sales tax, after taxing gasoline, tobacco and alcohol, he had to look for something else. He decided Canadians were making too many long-distance calls and added a 10 per cent tax on those starting January 1, 1988. When you live in Toronto or Montreal you can reach two or three million people without making long-distance calls. The population is large and for your monthly fee you can reach millions of people. However, if you have the luck to live in remote areas like the Gaspe or the Northwest Territories you have to call long-distance much more than when you live in Toronto or Montreal. This 10 per cent tax on long-distance calls has a big effect on people living in the regions. The Government will raise close to $1 billion through that tax every year.
As well, on the consumer side, the Government has decided to shift the sales tax to the wholesale level and the same rate of 12 per cent will raise a lot more money than the 12 per cent at the manufacturing level. So much for consumption taxes.

Mr. Speaker, apart from consumption taxes, there have been income tax increases as a result of discounting the first 3 per cent of inflation. Without saying a word about it, without passing any legislation, without referring to it in his Budget speech, the Minister of Finance will take this year just under $750 million from Canadian taxpayers. This was not mentioned in the Budget speech. It is not without reason that I stated in my comments that the Minister of Finance had not kept his promise. Not only did he fail to do so by adding new taxes in each successive Budget, but he has also failed in his promise in a roundabout way, through the back door, by partially deindexing income tax tables, which is bringing the Government $750 million a year without a single word being said about it!
Mr. Speaker, there have been a whole series of measures: The partial deindexation of family allowances, the partial deindexation of the child tax credit, lowering the ceiling for the child tax credit, and so on. Mr. Speaker, I would like the Minister to explain something to me. When you add up all those measures, you get something like $22 billion in tax increases. Why is it, after having increased taxes by $22 billion and after the six years of economic recovery mentioned by the Minister, that he still needs to borrow $25.3 billion for the coming fiscal year?
If I were involved in a boxing match, Mr. Speaker, I would tell the referee to keep his eyes open, that someone is hitting me hard, for this Minister has increased the taxes. He claims that he has cut Government expenditures and that he has to seek $25.3 billion in borrowing authority. Yet, Mr. Speaker,
Borrowing Authority
we do not have the estimates, only total figures. We do not know just how much will go to this or that department or agency. We have nothing of that.
Mr. Speaker, we are certainly not going to let the House adopt Bill C-109 unless we get at least some information about the manner in which this Tory Government intends to spend not only the money it is now borrowing, but also all the old and new taxes which the Government is collecting every year. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pleasure that I rise on behalf of the New Democratic Party to speak on this particular Bill. This Bill seeks to borrow the sum of $25.3 billion over the next fiscal year. The figure comes from $22.3 billion in the Budget, which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced on Wednesday, and a contingency fund of $3 billion on top of that for a total of $25.3 billion.
In my speech I will combine my remarks on this Bill and on the Budget since they are intertwined. I will also put forward the views of my constituents in Vancouver-Kingsway. However, that riding is to be eliminated in redistribution and if the election is held after July of this year, that riding will no longer exist. Therefore, I will also try to articulate the views of people who live in the area of Port Moody-Coquitlam in Vancouver, those wonderful people in the riding in which I will run if indeed we go on the new boundaries. Many of the same problems are shared by those people. Indeed, the people of Port Moody-Coquitlam share problems with many people all across the country with the present economy and the present policies of the Government.
We in the New Democratic Party believe that the Government's 1988 Budget is a Budget of lost opportunities. It was not the time to stand pat but a time for action. The Minister of Finance had a real opportunity to move to greater regional fairness, to stop the rising interest rates, and to make the tax system fairer. The latter is of particular concern because, except for the large corporations which do not pay any taxes at all, Canadians pay taxes which are taken right off the top of their wage packets. They are the ones who wanted a fairer taxation system. Instead, the Minister of Finance chose to have a stand-pat Budget that does little for the average Canadian family.
The Budget provides for an increase in the gasoline tax of one cent a litre, which will cost the average family $50 a year.
1 want to begin by referring to that gasoline tax. Since I have been the New Democratic Party energy critic for some seven years, I have seen a seemingly endless increase in this tax. The Government appears to consider the Canadian motorist as a milk cow because it seems to add another cent a litre gasoline
February 12, 1988

tax in every Budget in order to raise another S3 or $4 million from the motorist.
I visited Toronto last weekend where, we are told, the economy is booming. It is one area of the country where the economy seems to be pretty high, but once one scratches the surface and considers the average family, one sees that most families cannot afford to live in downtown Toronto but must live in the suburbs and drive to work. The same situation is faced by many Canadians who live in the larger cities, including Vancouver where many people live in the Coquitlam area and must drive to work. One of the problems there is that they need additional rapid transit to help them get to work.
While the Government put a tax on gasoline, there is no quid pro quo, an earmarking of $300 million, for example, to upgrade the rapid transit system.
Some of the local mayors in the riding of Port Moody- Coquitlam, particularly the mayor of Port Moody and the mayor of Port Coquitlam, have been advocating that Canadian Pacific Railway permit the upgrading and the use of its lines, with some help from the federal Government, to support a rapid transit system into Vancouver. This would save money and travel time for their residents.
However, what action did the Government take? It added another cent a litre tax at the pump without earmarking that money for improvements. Many Canadians live close to the border and know that our price for gasoline is almost double that in the United States. There are two reasons for this. The first is that the Government continues to add taxes at the pump, to which provincial governments add the so-called ad valorem tax.
The second reason is that oil companies make too much money and have too great a profit margin on their gasoline. The five big companies that control the gasoline market in Canada represent a classic oligopoly. They continue to increase the price of gasoline, sometimes at the same time as the Government increases its tax. We may see the oil companies tag on an increase to the price of gas as a result of this recent tax.
Eventually Canadian motorists and consumers will say that enough is enough. We in the New Democratic Party suggested that one approach to energy policy would be to reinvest money as a result of an additional cent a litre tax at the gas pump into such things as rapid transit or possibly to help small Canadian-owned oil companies by establishing a floor price for them, for example, so they will still be in existence when we experience our next energy crisis. This would also prevent the oil industry from being taken over completely by the multinational oil companies, as is happening now.
The Government continues to increase gasoline tax. This is the fourth increase since the Conservatives were elected in 1984 and the cumulative impact has been $350 for every family that uses a car. This Budget gave the Government an opportunity to correct the unfairness in the tax reform package
Borrowing Authority
of last year. However, the Government did not take advantage of that and the result is that in 1988 the average family will be paying more than $1,100 in additional taxes than in 1984. Only the richest 2 per cent of taxpayers will pay less.
The rich will get a break and the middle class, who are basically assuming the tax burden in this country, will be paying an additional $1,100. During Question Period today the finance critic for the new Democratic Party, the Hon. member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), asked questions about a minimum corporate tax. Even Ronald Reagan can do that, so why cannot the Government in Canada impose such a tax?
Let me give some figures which we have compiled. Under the Conservative tax regime, the following very profitable corporations paid no taxes in the most recent year for which such information is available. In 1986, Alcan Aluminum had profits totalling $220 million and even received a tax credit of $32 million. Brascan had profits of $187 million in 1986 and received a tax credit of $2.3 million. Hees International had profits totalling $117 million in 1986 and did not pay any taxes. In 1986, Power Financial had profits of $132 million and received a tax credit of $1 million. Xerox Canada had profits totalling $115 million in 1986 and received a tax credit of $10.8 million. In 1986, Total Petroleum, on profits totalling $40 million, received a tax credit of $2.2 million.
In 1986 Wardair had profits of $70 million, with no taxes paid. In 1986 Pacific Western had profits of $39 million with no income tax paid. Repap Enterprises had profits totalling $34 million in 1986, with no taxes paid. Union Carbide had profits of $28 million in 1986, with no taxes paid.
Bramalea had $51 million in profits with no taxes paid. In 1987, Cadillac Fairview had profits of $95 million and received a tax credit of $12.4 million. In 1987, Carena-Bancorp paid no taxes on profits totalling $37 million. In 1987, the Hudson's Bay Company had $50 million in profits and received a tax credit of $15.7 million. SICO Camp had profits totalling $43 million in 1987, with no taxes paid.
The average worker in this country has taxes taken directly off the pay cheque. I talked to a crane operator recently who got a terrific job and made $2,000. He received a cheque of $1,000. He does not get a tax credit because it comes directly from his cheque. That is what the average Canadian family is saying is unfair.
The Government continues to resist meaningful tax reform in this area. The Minister of Finance had an opportunity to bring in a minimum corporate tax that would ensure that all profitable corporations pay their fair share. It is not meant to tax them out of existence, but to have them pay their fair share.
The revenue generated from such a tax could be used for such things as regional development. Yet, with this Budget,
60,000	corporations will continue to pay no tax.
That raises the other problem of regional development in this country. There are essentially two Canada's. One is the

February 12, 1988
Borrowing Authority
area in the Golden Elorseshoe in Ontario which has a booming economy, even though there are housing problems. The second Canada includes the rest of the country where the boom has not arrived. My own province has an 11 per cent unemployment rate. That is too high.
In an afternoon news broadcast in my province yesterday, it was reported that the school board received permission to apply to the federal Government for funds to feed hungry children. Hopefully, there will be no more hungry children in the schools. There is desperation in our province. We have food banks in Vancouver. Some people are better off, but many people are still unemployed. It affects the vast majority of people in the workforce as well because it is difficult for them to move from one job to another or to seek higher wages. It is difficult for them to make any kind of changes at all. It is difficult to commit themselves to a high interest, long-term mortgage to buy a house because they may get dumped from their jobs, and it is very difficult to find another job in the labour market in British Columbia.
The Budget also ignores that half of the jobs created since the Government came to power have really been in one province with about one third of the population of the country. The Government is well intentioned in trying to create jobs. We all want to see that. But when the Government throws out figures of how many millions of jobs it has created, it should remember that those jobs tend to be in a certain region of the country. We are not against that, but we want to see some regional fairness. Second, the jobs which have been created tend to be lower paid jobs in the service industry. One should realize the kind of jobs the Government has created.
My Party and I believe that Canadians were looking for fairness in the Budget, but nothing is offered to close the growing disparity between people in central Canada and those in the outlying regions of Canada, in the east, west and north. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) warned us last year that we are in the process of building two Canadas, one which is rich and promising and one which is underdeveloped and underemployed. It seems to me this warning remains true today. But the Minister of Finance has lost the opportunity to do something about it.
Major improvements in job creation, I believe, are being held back because of the preoccupation of the Bank of Canada with interest rates. In order to get the economic growth to continue in the regions, we need a policy of regional fairness and development and we need a policy of lower interest rates.
The Economic Council of Canada has said that a cut in interest rates would be the single most job creating initiative the Government could undertake and that it would provide for far better growth for the economy than the proposed trade deal. Economists like Michael McCracken of Informetrica have argued for lower rates to stimulate the growth and counter the possibility of economic decline following the stock
market slide in October. But the Finance Minister continues to support the stance of the Governor of the Bank of Canada and has done nothing in his Budget to stimulate regional growth or lower interest rates which are, in my view, the most pressing economic problem in Canada.
The Canadian dollar has gone up so the Minister need not worry. He should forget about the old argument that we have to keep interest rates high to get foreign capital to come in and keep our dollar from falling. The time is right now to lower interest rates. That would help suburban families, the kind of family who lives in Port Moody or Coquitlam, who could afford a house and have more money left over because they would save on their mortgage payments.
I would like to conclude by addressing two further matters, first, the trade deal because it is tied in with the Budget. I cannot go into great detail about it, but I would say that many people in British Columbia were hoping that the trade deal would provide some answers for them. Many still assume that the deal provides the answer they wanted, that is, access to the American market. There would be unrestricted access to the goods and raw materials of British Columbia to the American market. But I say to them and to you, Mr. Speaker, that the fault with the Mulroney-Reagan trade deal is that it does not secure that access. In fact, it was a bad deal. Congress can still put countervails on our shakes and shingles and potash. It can still interfere with our logging and wood product exports. That is going to happen after the trade deal. So we have to ask ourselves, just as Canadians in British Columbia are asking themselves, what did we gain from this trade deal when we look at what we supposedly gained, access to the American market, which we did not, and compare it to what we gave up? We have entered into a continental energy policy. We have given away all our ace cards, all the control over our resources.
I think it is a bad deal. That is a developing debate in British Columbia.
What we are going to need instead is for Canadians to do it on their own with a regional development program and a Canadian national development project so that we can provide full employment in this country. We in the New Democratic Party have put out a paper written by my friend, the Hon. Member for Essex-Windsor (Mr. Langdon), our trade critic. It is called "A Time To Choose, the New Democrat's Trade Option in Canada". I do not have time to go through it right now but I will say that we believe there are other ways of keeping what we believe in strongly, of stimulating the economy and providing jobs, than joining in an economic union with the United States, which will ultimately lead to a political union.
I mentioned some corporations which did not pay taxes. I mentioned the gasoline tax which is hosing the consumer again. I want to conclude by going through some figures to show what has happened to the average family since this Government took power. I am talking about an average family with two children earning an income of $35,000.
February 12, 1988

In November 1984 in the Government's economic statement there was an increase in the oil and gas prices. That cost $200, unemployment insurance premiums another $102, and sales tax increases another $150. That totals $450. In May of 1985 we had a Budget. There was an elimination of federal tax reduction. That was $100. Indexing was modified for $115. There was a cut in family allowance payments, $22.50. Cigarette and alcohol increases cost $75. Sales tax was broadened, which cost $150. There was another gas tax increase, $50. That was another $512.
In 1986 we had another Budget. There was a 3 per cent surtax, $170, a sales tax increase, $150, a cigarette and alcohol tax increase, $20. That is $340. In 1987, another Budget with another gas increase, $50, sales tax broadened, $15, cigarette and air tax increased, $35. So we are up to about $80 there.
On June 18, 1987, the tax reform comes in. There are changes in the tax categories, so we have to subtract $310. Now we have this Budget with the increase in gasoline tax, another $50. All this totals $1,124.50. That is the increase for the average family since this Government took office. I challenge the Government to deal with that and I challenge the Government to go to the country and face the average Canadian family who wants to see some fairness in taxes and in regional disparity. The Government should make this the kind of fair system that Canadians have come to expect.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a brief comment and ask the Hon. Member to respond to it. 1 want to express my satisfaction with the Hon. Member's speech. He clearly outlined the problems that the one cent per litre increase in tax on gasoline would present to the people in the suburban areas of Vancouver, an area he represents, as well as people living in other large cities.
I would like to point out how it really hits areas such as the one I represent in Prince Edward Island, which is a rural area, where farmers and fishermen and those who can find jobs have to drive 30, 40 and 50 kilometres one way to and from their work or their place of shopping. Indeed, just to attend church services these people have to drive that many kilometres. An automobile is not a luxury anymore in those areas. It is a necessity. It is something that the citizens of the country have to rely on.
Another point that came out in the Budget was that farmers and fishermen will be exempt from this one cent per litre increase. I would like the Hon. Member to comment on this point as well. It is a very misleading statement because farmers and fishermen are also consumers. While they are exempt in terms of their on- farm activities and their fishing industry activities, they are still consumers. They still have to travel miles to and from their shopping areas and to all the other activities that they as ordinary citizens have to do.
I just want to set the record clear today. It is not quite right to say that farmers and fishermen are exempt. While they are
Borrowing Authority
exempt in their own farm activities, they are not exempt anymore than anyone else when it comes to their ordinary daily lives. Will the Hon. Member please make a comment on that point?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree with the Hon. Member with respect to farmers and fishers. He is exactly right. He also brings out the point that Canadians drive to work. In that respect 1 mentioned the suburbs. But in some cases such as in Prince George, British Columbia, if someone has to drive to a mill it is often out of town. In Pouce Coupe people have to drive to their work there. I will not advocate cheap gasoline prices. I think the American prices are too low. There is room for some taxation there and there will be some. The Americans will eventually get around to it.
There is also an argument for conservation when consumers have to pay a great deal for gasoline. Environmentalists will make that argument. There has to be a bit of a trade-off. I often find that the environmentalists who make that argument live right next to the Bloor Street subway line in Toronto. They do not live in Prince George where they would have to drive 30 miles to the mill. So we have to need a fair saw-off if you like.
What is happening is that the Government has reached the point where the consumer, the motorist, has become a milk cow. In every Budget it seems that there is another one cent per litre tax imposed. When I was energy critic, I used to know what I was going to say even before the Budget was tabled. I did not even have to see it. If someone asked me to comment on it, I could say that this is what they will be doing to the motorists. It was right all the time.
I think that at some point in time the Government will see rebellion from the motorists who will say, "Look, it is just too much". Motorists may be prepared to pay more if they thought that the money was going for something, not just for a Tory slush fund for an election or a pay-out here to let Grant Devine win an election. If they thought that it was earmarked for energy development, for conservation, for regional development or for rapid transit then they would probably agree to it. But the consumers, including the fishermen and the farmers, will not be fooled anymore. They will start to rebel on this point.
The former Minister of Finance, the Hon. Member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) had a nasty experience when he tried to hose Canadians at the pump too fast. This time the Government is stretching out the agony. Canadians will be in agony nevertheless at the pumps. They will rebel at this point.

Mr. Speaker, there a number of matters that could be included there. High interest rates make it harder for us in British Columbia to compete with the United States. The cost of financing our new investment now is 30 per cent higher than it is in the United States. Thus companies are locating south of the border rather than in Canada.
There have been a number of bankruptcies as a result of the high interest rates. The number of families who could not afford mortgages to buy homes has meant that economic development has not progressed because of the high interest rates.
The Government has to make a decision. Does it choose between ordinary Canadians who would benefit from low interest rates or does it protect its friends, whether it is in the oil industry or a certain group of Canadians who feel that inflation is the big problem and they want those particular investments protected? With our policy, which advocates lower interest rates, it would stimulate development. It would use the Government and not leave everything to the so-called free market. It would use the Government in partnership with private industry. It would use the tools of the Government to help in regional development to encourage it rather than putting all our eggs in the American basket. This would give us an independent economic policy and an independent foreign policy as well as an independent cultural policy.
Those are all part of our vision of Canada. We in the New Democratic Party think that that is the real alternative for Canada. We think that the place to start is in the economic arena. We will keep up pressure on this. The Government should tackle the Bank of Canada on the interest rates and force them down. It seems to us that this would be to the benefit of ordinary Canadians. The economy needs this or else we will go into another economic slump.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member has given a good answer to the question of how lowering the interest rates would benefit the regions of Canada. Can he be more specific about the region in which he has his representation, that is, within British Columbia?
What I have in mind is that in downtown Toronto, which I represent, we have two kinds of banks. We have the banks on Bay Street, which are the beneficiaries, as he said, of the high interest rates. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. Our big problem in British Columbia is that we have not diversified our economy which is still concentrated in mining, forestry and so on. We also export raw materials. When those industries are all right we have boom times, but when times are bad that is when we have bust times.
Increasingly, with other competitors across the world, those good times will not come back. We have to diversify our economy. We have to produce some of our mining machinery at home and sell it to the world. Similarly, with our forest industry, and so on. We have to develop some type of manufacturing industry to provide for our local people, and to use our raw materials and export those raw materials, especially to the Asia-Pacific market. There is a regional strategy for the Pacific region that makes sense.
It cannot be done when high interest rates are skimming off money and investment, and basically putting it in the hands of the big banks on Bay Street. We know that the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) are basically two boys from Bay Street, both corporate lawyers who represent the interests of the big banks and the big companies. Whether it is a Liberal or a Conservative Government, that is why we will always have high interest rates and policies that will not be for regional development. With the policies that we prefer, led by lower interest rates and by encouragement for regional development and stimulus in using the powers of the Government of Canada, we can have development in the riding of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), and we think we can also have it in my riding in British Columbia.
If there was a New Democratic Government in this country, there would be a fair system of taxation, and there would not be one food bank left in the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in the debate today on Bill C-209, which is an Act to provide a borrowing authority, I am somewhat amazed that the Government would expect those of us in the House, and Canadians in general, to accept the fact that it was going to ask to borrow $25.3 billion without even telling us what it is for. When most individuals in this House, and most Canadians throughout the land go to a bank, they do not get a blank cheque until they have some reason for borrowing the money. We should not be offering the Government a blank cheque until we have seen the Estimates and know exactly where it intends to spend this $25.3 billion.
Debate on this Bill coming directly after Wednesday's Budget heightens my disappointment with the performance of the Government, its spending, and taxation proposals. The Budget is certainly one of missed opportunities. It could
February 12, 1988

certainly have done some good for Canadians in promoting job creation and in fairness, the types of things that we think would be fair and equitable from a balanced Canadian view, and which would enable people to live with a great deal more security in this country.
Through this Budget, the Tories have demonstrated their lack of deep commitment to the cultural community activities. Today that is what I wish to focus on in attacking and asking the Government to take a look at where it will be spending the $25 billion extra that it will borrow. 1 want to know where it will be put, and in particular I would like to address the whole area of the cultural community. That is a very large constituency. They are the people who help to define us, explain us, and speak to us and for us in a very significant way.
I wish to point out that, for the cultural sector of our society, the November, 1984 economic statement presented us with $122.5 million in major cuts to all levels of federal expenditures. If that wasn't bad enough, and indicated their strong and deep commitment-if you pardon the sarcasm-to the cultural industries, let us take a look at what was done in May,
1985.	I guess the Government was embarrassed because that community was spared any further cuts. However, in February, 1986, the Government started to repay for some of its sins of omission and it gave an allocation of $75 million over the next five years through dedicated programs. In 1987 there was absolutely no attempt at restoring the Government's earlier cuts. Now in 1988 in this Wilson Budget, we are told that there will be further reductions of $300 million in annual expenditures, but we do not know exactly where.
We do not have any details or explanations. The question is, will it be straight cuts and reductions across all programs and agencies? Will that be the fair approach, or will the Government pick and choose its friends, its winners and losers, or will certain agencies and programs be singled out to receive higher cuts? I think that Canadians will have to look very carefully'at these Estimates and find out what the BBC boys and girls will be saying.
When I say the BBC, I am talking about the Back Bench Club who have some very interesting views of society. I would say dinosaur views.
Let us look at one particular area that seems of concern. The Government announced its intention to remove the provisions in the Income Tax Act that currently apply to the withholding tax to payments for the use in Canada of film and video tapes used in connection with news material gathered by foreign sources in our television programming.
At first glance this provision does not seem dramatic. It is the removal of a 10 per cent tax which provides the Government with somewhere around a million dollars. We do not have the actual figure. But this action will allow broadcasters an opportunity to obtain foreign news cheaper than at present.
Was this provision one that would assist the private sector in its bid for an all-news licence? I wonder if this was instituted
Borrowing Authority
as part of a side deal made with the Americans during the free trade talks in order that we could gather in more and more information from an American perspective. It is not American bashing, Mr. Speaker, that I am concerned about. It is the assimilation of American lifestyle, thinking, and action as the only way to look at the world. We are not Americans. We are Canadians. We have our own perspective. We have our own sense of what is right and wrong. That is what we want to see on our film screen. When we turn on the television set to watch the news, we want to see Canadian news from a Canadian perspective.
By removing the 10 per cent tax on films and videos that come from the United States, instead of encouraging an indigenous Canadian industry to flourish, in essence the Government has not contributed in any way to Canadian culture. It has only promoted the whole eyes and ears of Americans focusing in on Canada, absorbing their perspective, their viewpoints from their history and from their values. If that is a contribution to Canadian culture, then I believe that it is not the way that one would want to serve Canadians and Canadian values, and particularly Canadian sovereignty.
If the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) was asking to borrow $25.3 billion and he included some expenses for some of his Party's commitments, then perhaps it would not be so discomforting or incompatible with the verbiage and the rhetoric to which we have been subjected since 1984.
Let us take a look at what the Tories had to say to us during the 1984 election when they made those wonderful strong commitments to Canadian culture. I would remind all Members who were Progressive Conservative candidates that six commitments were made in this area, together with the 360 some odd that were made in general.
The first was to maintain federal funding of cultural agencies in line with inflation. The second was to provide real growth in federal contributions to the cultural sector. The third was to look for other sources of funding for the arts councils and the cultural agencies such as tax credits. The fourth was to look for further financial assistance for the cultural sector by widening the sorts of enterprises which qualified under investment incentive criteria. The fifth was a thorough examination of cultural agencies such as the CBC, Telefilm, and the National Arts Centre. That was done through the Nielsen study and a few other studies, which I will come to. The sixth was the commitment to traditional arm's length relationships between Government and the cultural agencies. Let us see how the Government met its promises, its rhetoric, and its commitments.
First, in respect of the maintenance of federal funding and the provision of real growth, neither of these commitments has been met. In fact, the reverse has happened. In the 1984 economic statement there was a total loss of $122.5 million to the sector, and cultural agencies parliamentary appropriations

February 12, 1988
Borrowing Authority
have not kept pace with inflation to this day. In 1987 the National Arts Centre received an actual 4.1 per cent decrease in real terms in its parliamentary allocation. In 1987 the Canada Council received a .1 per cent decrease in its appropriation. The CBC, our major cultural agency, suffered a staggering decline of 13 per cent in its spending since this Government took office. The amount of money available to the CBC today is only 87 per cent of what it was in real terms when this Government took over.
Instead of trying to stab it, snub it, or snuff it, I would suggest that the CBC be looked at and accredited with the incredible growth and development of all arts and cultural personalities and products in the country. Where else was there to grow and to be a national instrument which encouraged the development of Canadian talent in all sectors of cultural interest and all key support sectors such as film crews, editors, writers, creators in every field?
In that sense we can forget about the first two commitments. Let us turn to the third and fourth commitments, incentives to new funding sources. To this I can only say that instead of looking for new sources of funding, once again they have chipped away at existing provisions. This time it was at the 100 per cent capital cost allowance for films, which was finally enabling risk capital in a productive way. I have heard some people say that they were producing schlock or high art. Well, we should have the right to do all that here in Canada. If there are people who have the ability and foresight to see that this is a very good industry for Canada, they should be encouraged to do so. Instead the 100 per cent capital cost allowance for films was reduced to 30 per cent. That is no incentive. We can do better with mining shares.
Along with this situation we have the Government's inability to produce Canadian film legislation that will recognize Canadian film rights and give us an indigenous industry. This cut, along with some of the other things the Government has done, is putting the nail in the coffin of ever being able to develop a film industry indigenous to Canada. It is bending to American will, the voice of Jack Valenti whispered strongly into the ear of Ronald Reagan.
Turning to the fifth point, they wanted to do a thorough examination of cultural agencies, such as the CBC, Telefilm, and the National Arts Centre. Well, they have done that. The former Minister of Communications certainly went out of his way on this promise. Let us remember the task forces-the task force on broadcasting at a cost of $2.8 million, the task force on national museums at a cost of $425,000, the task force on funding of the arts at a cost of $833,000, the task force on the film industry at a cost of $134,000, the task force on the National Arts Centre for $319,000, and the task force on the status of the artist at a cost of $50,000. Of course these are in addition to the Nielsen task force. In three and a half years of Conservative Government, there have been six major task forces and many other studies undertaken at a total cost in excess of $4.5 million.
What have been the results? Not only did the task forces make very credible suggestions to the House for consideration and action, but the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture tabled approximately 11 reports in the House. We have talked to the federal museum policy, the National Archives issue, and the Canadian broadcasting policy, but the Government has not cared to look at a single issue that we addressed. They have been ignored. If some of the Government's borrowing funds go toward meeting the needs addressed in the $4.5 million worth of study, not to speak of the cost of running the parliamentary committees and the open hearings we have had, at least then I would feel that we were a little better protected.
What about the last commitment, the commitment to the traditional arm's length relationship between government and cultural agencies? If the recent interference in the CRTC licensing of the CBC all-news service is arm's length, then I would suggest that the shoulder is moving down to the wrist. We have seen the most interventionist action ever in respect of the independent Board of Directors of the CBC, careful research, open hearings, and decision making of the quasitribunal members of the CRTC.
If. instead of spending some $11 billion or $12 billion on nuclear submarines, the Government could have taken action in a few really concrete ways, we would have had something more exciting to present to the cultural sector.
I have a few suggestions for the Minister of Finance before he prints his Estimates for artists and individual creators. 1 would suggest that the Income Tax Act be amended to define the term "professional artist" in line with the criteria set out in Revenue Canada's interpretation bulletin IT-504 and to define such other related terms as might be required. The standing committee made this recommendation to the Government as has. the arts community over past years. The basis of the recommendation indicates that we should recognize artists in a defined class. We should not leave them to the whims of the court. They should be given special recognition under the Income Tax Act, and the definitions in IT-504 should be used as they are acceptable to the arts community and to Revenue Canada. They could certainly be used to have force of law protection for the artists instead of having them subject to whims and interpretations which are not always fair and well guided.
For the Government to do this would not be very difficult. The work has been done. The definitions are there. Current administrative criteria and recasting them for inclusion in The Canada Gazette would entail no new policy decisions. It would just be an adoption of new language which is seemingly difficult for the Department of Justice to put together. However, none of it is really that technical. From the point of view of the arts community, this approach would mean that the definitions would have status and would have far more authority than mere administrative guidelines. Further, the applicable guidelines could be cited in a court and could then

be used in decisions which might be difficult to arrive at under present guidelines, if they were embodied in the statute.
Frankly I find unacceptable the removal of the right of professional artists to use block averaging and the modified accrual basis of accounting. In June the Government proposed abolishing all averaging provisions. Mr. Speaker, are you indicating that I have one minute left?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PEACE-MAKING ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING TAX CREDIT
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PEACE-MAKING ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, in pursuance of a stated policy of peace and peace-making, the government should consider the advisability of establishing a 100 per cent tax credit which would allow residents of Canada who pay income tax, to transfer a portion of their tax to recognized Canadian or International agencies which conduct peace research, peace education or development projects aimed at promoting peaceful understanding in regions of conflict, such credit to be 100 per cent of the amount so transferred up to a maximum of the percentage of the national budget allocated to defence which is projected at 9.39 per cent for the coming year.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on Motion No. 112. The effect of this motion would be to allow Canadians who pay income tax to transfer the portion of it which normally would go to defence purposes to a fund or
Peace-making
series of funds that would be recognized by the Government and devoted to peace purposes, peace education, peace research or some kind of development program that would encourage the peaceful resolution of conflict in other parts of the world. This is the third time I have raised a motion similar to this for debate in the House of Commons.
Is is an idea that will some day be turned into reality. I hope that someday we will be able to turn it into reality in this House of Commons, perhaps even today if Members opposite are willing to consider this on its merits.
It is an idea that is being considered by people around the world as an alternative to the unacceptable measures of militarism which are not leading to peace and security in the world today. It is an idea that we recognize is never particularly popular with the Government. It was not acceptable to the Liberal Government-

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PEACE-MAKING ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING TAX CREDIT
speechtext: Has anybody passed it in the world yet?

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PEACE-MAKING ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Nobody in the world that I am aware of has passed it. That does not mean that it is not an idea that has merit. The fact that nobody before Galileo and Copernicus recognized that the world was round did not mean that it was flat, did it? The fact that nobody in the world has passed this yet does not mean that it is not a worth-while idea.
There are two reasons behind this motion. First, it is to give effect to the concern of Canadians for freedom of conscience. Freedom of conscience is recognized in our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Second, it is to provide an alternative to militarism. I would like to speak about both of these in turn.
Freedom of conscience is the first freedom that is guaranteed in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. Yet we have never really defined what it means to Canadians. There is no question of conscience that is more central to people in Canada or anywhere else in the world than the relationship of individuals to the state, particularly with regard to the question of waging war.
This particular relationship of conscience has a long history. Dr. Jerilynn Prior is one of the people who is in the forefront of the struggle for freedom of conscience. She has appeared before the courts on this issue and has laid before the courts a document entitled Peace Testimony of the Society of Friends, a declaration the harmless and innocent people of God called Quakers presented to Charles II in 1660. This declaration reads:
WE UTTERLY DENY all outward wars and strife, and fightings with outward weapons, for any end, or under any pretence whatever; this is our testimony to the whole world. The Spirit of Christ by which we are guided is not changeable, so as once to command us from a thing as evil, and again to move unto it; and we certainly know, and testify to the world, that the Spirit of Christ, which leads us into all truth, will never move us to fight and war against any man with outward weapons, neither for the kingdom of Christ, nor for the kingdoms of this world.
This declaration made before Charles II was backed up by the lives of the Quakers, the Society of Friends, who refused to

February 12, 1988
Peace-making
go to war. Many of them were willing to go to prison rather than to go to war.
There are other historic peace churches including the Mennonites and the Hutterites who have had a long history of refusing to be involved in militarism. Canada has recognized that right over the years, particularly during the First World War and the Second World War when we recognized the status of conscientious objector. People who, on the basis of conscience, declared that they could not go to war were able to register as conscientious objectors and were put to some other useful work in the world. These people made a great contribution. No one can accuse them of cowardice or of not being good citizens. Rather, they are the very best of citizens because they see that good citizenship entails acting within the dictates of one's own conscience. They refuse to let their conscience be commanded by any state.
We are now dealing with an extension of the principle that people should not be forced to go to war against their conscience. We extend that to the principle that they should not be forced to pay for war or militarism against their conscience. In order to give effect to that, there is an organization called Conscience Canada which, over the last five years, has set up a peace tax trust fund in which people are encouraged to put that portion of their taxes which would normally go for defence purposes. Over the last five years, some 370 people have placed over SI09,000 in that trust fund.
Perhaps we could get a better idea of what these people are thinking if 1 read from letters written by some of them. Mr. Wolfgang Blach of Montreal writes:
I am doing this because I cannot agree to participate financially in the preparation of war, even indirectly through taxes. I also hope that this will press your government and mine to legislate provisions which would make this procedure official. Until that time 1 have to base my action on the Charter of Rights' freedom of conscience guarantee.
Proposals to this effect have already been tabled in the House of Commons. It has not been taken seriously, probably because it came from across the floor. Please do not play war games in the house. If you think the proposal is inadequate, suggest amendments, but I urge you to at least consider such a bill with all the seriousness this non-partisan issue warrants.
Another letter came from D. Craig Summers of Kingston, Ontario, who writes:
Nuclear weapons scare me. They have made our continued existence on Earth more precarious than when there were none. The present push by our "neighbours" to the south for a Star Wars safety shield also escalates our danger. Furthermore, the testing of US submarines at Nanoose Bay, BC, and the production of Cruise Missile components at Litton Industries in Toronto exemplify Canada's involvement in preparations for mass destruction. This is unacceptable, and the list goes on and on.
Peace and international security will be found in equally sharing the vast resources of our earth, not through the most powerful nations coercing people into paying for military systems which threaten to destroy all of us, in order to maintain their political advantage and control. By paying taxes to the military,
I feel as if I am killing people myself. In good conscience, I cannot allow my taxes to support such madness.
Dr. Jerilynn Prior who, as I mentioned earlier, is involved in a test case before the courts right now, said:
As a person of conscience who would refuse to fight in a war on moral and
religious grounds, I also refuse to pay for war on the same grounds. My
constitution allows me freedom of conscience.
As I mentioned earlier, this is an international movement. It involves Canada, the U.S., Australia, Japan, and a number of western European countries. The people involved are not seeking to evade their responsibilities as citizens of nations where the peace tax movement is growing. Rather, they want to meet their obligations as citizens in a way that does not do violence to their conscience.
Second, I want to speak to this motion as an alternative to the growing militarism of our world. There is no reference in the motion to questions of conscience. It is an open-ended motion and if the Government wants to take a very strict approach to this, it could bring in legislation that would make a peace tax credit available only to people of conscience who, on that basis, could not pay taxes that would be used for military purposes. It would be a measure that limited a peace tax credit only to people who objected on the grounds of conscience. That would be a noteworthy first step which I would welcome. Indeed, I would prefer to see a much more open proposal from the Government. There are people like myself who are not opposed on the strict level of conscience to any payment of taxes used for the military. I am not opposed to that personally. However, I am concerned about developing alternatives to the growing militarism that we see in Canada and around the world.
One of the concerns I have about the Mulroney-Reagan trade agreement is found in Article 2003 which exempts so-called essential security interests from the provisions of the deal. What that means is that Canadian programs to help the different regions, economic programs for the Maritimes, for example, or the North, can and will be subject to American pressures and could be ruled to be unacceptable subsidies. The American tradition of providing help for the regions through defence procurement contracts will be completely exempt from the provisions of the deal. That means that if Canada wants to offer some kind of help to its regions, it is going to be more and more pushed into taking the same approach and using military procurement contracts and defence industries as the one acceptable way under this trade agreement of getting aid out to the different regions.
This is one more way in which we see the growing militarization of the Canadian economy. We can see the same sort of thing on a global scale. In an address as President of the United States, Dwight D. Eisenhower said:
Every gun that is made, every warship launched, every rocket fired, signifies, in the final sense, a theft from those who hunger and are not fed, those who are cold and not clothed.
He continued:
This world in arms is not spending money alone; it is spending the sweat of its labourers, the genius of its scientists, the hopes of its children.
February 12, 1988

If anyone knew the reality of war it was President Eisenhower. He had been Supreme Commander of the Allied Forces during World War II. He spent his life in the American military. Yet he thought it necessary to warn about the danger of the military industrial complex and point to the danger of growing militarization.
We can look at what that kind of militarization does to the world's economy. The Brundtland report entitled "Our Common Future" has a whole chapter on peace and security. It points out that in 1985 the world spent well over $900 billion for military purposes. Today it would be over $1 trillion, or more than $2.5 billion a day. The report says:
The real cost is what the same resources might otherwise be used for:
An Action Plan for Tropical Forests would cost $1.3 billion a year over the course of five years. This annual sum is the equivalent of half a day of military expenditure world wide.
Implementing the UN Action Plan for Decertification would cost $4.5 billion a year during the last two decades of this century-the equivalent of less than two days of military spending.
One of the greatest environmental hazards in the Third World is lack of clean water for household use, contributing to 80 per cent of disease. The UN Water and Sanitation Decade, although given only a small fraction of support needed, would have cost $30 billion a year during the 1980s. This is the approximate equivalent of ten days of military spending.
To supply contraceptive materials to all women already motivated to use family planning would cost an additional $1 billion per year on top of the $2 billion spent today. This additional $1 billion is the equivalent of ten hours of military spending.
That is a distortion of world spending and it does not bring peace or security any closer. Quite the reverse. In the meantime, these other urgent needs are being neglected.
Surely there has to be some way for individual citizens to stand up and say to Governments that this stupidity has to stop. That is what this peace tax is all about. Militarism does not contribute to global security but to global insecurity. The intermediate missile agreement under which the U.S. and Russia agreed to scrap missiles contributed more to the peace of mind of the people of our world than all the billions of dollars spent to create those missiles in the first place. They are destroying something they built in order to guarantee peace in the world, yet the destruction of those missiles is the best move toward peace we have seen in recent years. Surely we should be able to grasp the irony of that situation. Yet we madly continue on this thrust to spend more money on militarization.
Veterans Against Nuclear Arms have emphasized the need for our world to develop an approach to common security. They have pointed to the folly and futility of our Government's policy of purchasing nuclear submarines. This is just not the answer to Canada's security needs. We need alternatives. No Party and no Government has a monopoly on stupidity or folly. Whatever Party is in Government, there has to be some provision so that individuals across Canada can suggest alternatives. That is what this motion does. It gives people a chance to vote with their money for some reasonable, sensible alternatives to growing militarism.
Peace-making
In conclusion, some people have raised the floodgate argument. If we have a peace tax provision, they say, it will open the door to all kinds of other special interest groups who will want an exemption from the tax. I would like to suggest two answers to that. First, we are talking about specific legislation for the peace tax. How many other issues would arise causing this particular kind of crisis of conscience? Perhaps one or two, I do not know. However, let them be debated and treated on their merit. Let us treat this issue on its merit.
Second, what would be so wrong in building flexibility into our tax system? We already do it for businesses. We do it for political Parties which get tax credits. We do it for charities. Why not for issues of conscience? We are talking about a policy of small steps where the people of Canada who believe in this approach would want to take the small step of working with some peace group to develop alternatives to militarism. In place of the present system I urge the Government to recognize the rights and conscience of the Canadian people and to recognize the contribution they could make to Canadian security if this measure was enacted.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have this opportunity to express my views on the motion of the Hon. We know that charitable organizations will profit from these tax credits the same way they were benefitting from deductions. I would venture saying that peace is an objective, if not the first at least a secondary one, of several charitable organizations.
We also know that, if they so wish, Canadian taxpayers can contribute to the United Nations. There again, such contributions will be treated the way I mentioned. There is no doubt in my mind that the basic principle behind the United Nations, and its main objective, is the promotion of peace. So I think that Canada is very well covered in that respect.
I heard my colleague talk about extending that amount to peace organizations and maybe two or three other about which we do not know yet but they will eventually be identified. At the same time, he asked for more flexibility into the Canadian

February 12, 1988
Peace-making
tax system. Instead of flexibility, Mr. Speaker, I believe that when introducing his tax reform last December, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has brought us more simplicity. If ever this Governement or this Parliament decided to strike a peace tax, plus other taxes concerning the two or three other elements that my colleague talked about, saying he did not know what they were but that, at some point, suggestions would be made to that effect, we would embark in a tax system that instead of being simplified would be once again far more complicated, and that is precisely what we do not want and precisely why we have been presented a corporate and personal tax reform.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the previous Liberal Government used to enjoy bringing into every Budget seven or eight new measures that would further complicate the system, and introducing into the Income Tax Act all kinds of social measures, measures affecting culture, regional development and so on, none of which would properly fit in an income tax legislation.

There are 282 Members in this House, Mr. Speaker, and I am convinced that if they were asked to come up with a definition there would be just as many answers. You can imagine the mess we would be in!
Again, Mr. Speaker, keeping in mind the fact that you may make a tax deductible contribution to United Nations-registered charitable organizations and claim a tax credit beginning in 1988 . . .
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, I had the pleasure of meeting with 120-odd students from Trois-Rivieres' Keranna School. These young girls came to Ottawa to see their Member of Parliament, of course, and we exchanged views concerning weapons, Cruise missiles and other issues of great interest to them. I told them that Canada's policy is to promote disarmament. I think that Canada is making a worthy contribution to support disarmament on the international scene, and hopefully time will come when people the world over will be talking about peace.
That is pretty well along the line of the motion introduced by the Hon. Member. We have accomplished a lot of work on the international scene, and we will continue to make progress in that field.
The Hon. Member advocates a special tax or a deduction for peace, it does not matter how he calls it, but the system is already in place. When it comes to disarmament Canada has made a name for itself in international quarters, Mr. Speaker, and I would suggest that we should not make any attempt to change a system which operates quite well and gives good results.
Mr. Speaker, instead of adopting the motion I think it might be a good idea to enquire whether the Hon. Member might have questions or comments concerning the point I have just raised.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   PEACE-MAKING ADVISABILITY OF ESTABLISHING TAX CREDIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal put forward today by the Hon. Member for Cowi-chan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) has an amazing principle involved with it. What he is really saying is that the Government should have the right to set tax rates and to determine how much might be payable by any one taxpayer. It is that taxpayer who is to determine how that money is actually to be spent. The taxpayer will instruct the Government how his or her tax dollars are to be spent according to his or her wishes.
The administrative problems alone, Sir, would be almost insurmountable. This is against the very purpose of the state's existence.
February 12, 1988

Why we as human beings have arranged our affairs so as to have various countries, varies states and provinces is so that we can undertake collective action on behalf of us all. In the perfect scheme of things, I suppose one would not need the state. The state would wither away, as has been suggested by people at certain times. But the simple fact of the matter is that, particularly for reasons like national defence, we need the institution of the state. I will return to this idea a little later in my dissertation.
If we were to let the Member get away with his suggestion this afternoon, what about the other side of the coin? Can we apply it vice versa? The Government of Canada spends a lot of money in the promotion of peace right now. A lot of our diplomatic efforts are designed for that end. We spend over SI billion on things like CIDA to try to promote peace and development throughout the world. What if someone objected to that and said they did not want their money spent on diplomatic peace initiatives or on CIDA, but preferred to have their tax money spent on armaments? Would we allow that? It is exactly, precisely the same argument.
In the very unlikely event that the NDP ever forms the Government of Canada, which I do not think will happen, what would happen? As I understand it, one of the first things that the NDP would do is institute a system of abortion clinics throughout Canada, paid for by the state. This is the goal that the Hon. Member supports. I do not know how he squares that with his conscience, but it is something that I could not support, in my conscience.
He spoke at length about freedom of conscience when he proposed his motion. If, God forbid, the NDP did come into power and did institute that, would it be possible for people to refuse that their taxes be used for that purpose and to declare that they want their taxes used for research on better methods of birth control? Is that what the Hon. Member or the New Democratic Party wants?
I understand as well that if the New Democratic Party ever got into office they would like to implement nationalization programs. I understand they would like to nationalize banks and oil companies. That is completely contrary to the way I think, but should I, as an individual whose view at that time would not represent the majority, be able to say that I do not want my tax dollars used for that purpose? I do not think the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands would agree with that.
Let us consider the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for a moment. I understand it uses about $800 million a year of taxpayers' money. Not all of us like all the programs that are put on CBC.

Should it be possible for someone to say: "I don't want certain of my tax dollars to be used by CBC to put Archie Bunker on TV because I would rather look at something else". Is that what the Hon. Member is suggesting? I am sure that he would say no. In a way, perhaps the answer to a question like that should be yes. I think there is a way that can be accomplished.
This leads me to the second point of my argument. I said before that the Government and the state is, of necessity, an instrument of coercion. It has to be in order to perform its function. It is important in areas such as national defence that all should bear a fair share of those necessary expenses.
However, when it comes to things like broadcasting, it seems to me that in those areas this is not necessary. If we have a free market in the maximum of areas, that is where we can have our individual choice. In my opinion, the state is involved in far too many things. The state should remove itself from many areas of human endeavour where it intervenes at present. That is how we can get an individual choice and have the concept of one dollar, one vote.
If the state was not involved in broadcasting a person could use his or her tax dollars that presently go toward the CBC to subscribe to the pay TV channel of his or her choice. In my opinion, that would be a good idea rather than letting the CBC and the state decide what is good for us to watch. People, themselves, can then choose. If people had the real choice, I wonder how many would prefer that their donation go to REAL Women, for example, rather than the National Action Committee where many tax dollars are spent at the present time.
How do we maximize individual freedom of choice, individual freedom of conscience as the Hon. Member supposedly would want to do? In my opinion, it is by minimizing the presence of government. That is the difference between the Conservative philosophy and the socialist philosophy. If the Hon. Member was really true to what he is saying, he would be running over to join us on this side of the House rather than sitting there with his socialist friends.

Mr. Speaker, 1 must say that the considerations on this important subject have also given us a general overview of all other issues that attract the concern of Canadians.
I would like personally to congratulate the Hon. Member who presented this motion. The Hon. Member is a practical man, and he realizes his motion will probably never be implemented.
However, my reason for commending his proposal is that the Hon. Member gives us an opportunity to air our thoughts and consider some very important current issues. I agree there is a
