vast difference between his views and the views of the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) who spoke earlier.

He said that is the difference between Conservatives and socialists. You may say that there is a difference between a progressive and a conservative. I do not understand why we should put abortion in this debate because to go through an abortion is such a painful and agonizing decision for a woman. I do not see why we should put that into a debate of the kind we have this afternoon, even though I totally disagree with the people who, after the Supreme Court judgment, celebrated with champagne because they won. I do not know what they won. I think this question is too painful to celebrate the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada.
On the subject matter raised by the Hon. Member, I want to say that I am extremely interested. That is why I stayed this afternoon.

-because the Hon. Member has once again given us an opportunity to reflect-as I am very fond of doing myself-on issues that should be very important to us, and I am referring to peace and security.
The Hon. Member for Trois-Rivieres (Mr. Vincent) said that Canada made its mark thanks to similar initiatives. 1 knew Mr. Pearson. I was elected under Mr. Pearson. I was elected under Mr. Trudeau. I am not a disciple of either man, even if I was a Member of Mr. Pearson's Government, but I have great respect for these two great Prime Ministers who have left their mark on the people and the youth of my generation by stressing the importance of these concerns.
In fact, I was Chairman of the Committee on Foreign Affairs and National Defence which had the privilege of reporting to the House on the last day the previous Liberal Government was in power. On Mr. Trudeau's last day as Prime Minister, I had the honour of reporting back to the House-in time, I may add-on a Bill he was very anxious to see adopted, and I am referring to the Bill to establish the Canadian Institute for International Peace and Security. 1 would urge Hon. Members to read Hansard, both for the remarks made by the Hon. Member-I will call her Ms. Jewett, because you know I don't like calling people by their riding, although I realize it is against the Standing Orders

 and for what Mr. Trudeau had to say that day.
So if young Canadians would like to read an interesting debate, they should look at what was said on June 27, 28 and 29, 1984. These are approximate dates, Mr. Speaker. These debates led to the establishment of the Institute for Peace and Security. For the benefit of the Hon. Member who spoke before me, I would say this proves that the previous Government was concerned about both security and peace problems in the world.
I do not see why the Hon. Member should be blamed for forcing us, on a Friday afternoon when most Members have already made a hasty return trip to their ridings, I hope, not on holidays ... I for one will be in my riding all week .. . but to meet with our constituents during the mid-winter break. Like you, Mr. Speaker, I will go to my riding, but I know one thing, namely that the issue is important enough to justify my staying here late into the afternoon, to force us together openly in front of Quebecers who are listening to me-

-in front of Canadians who should be interested in this question of peace and security and how to achieve it. So I am certainly not going to blame the Hon. Member for obliging some of us to reflect on how we could help to find a solution to the problems of tomorrow.
We live in a world of pure madness where more and more and more we believe we can create jobs by spending billions of dollars on ammunition. When we talk about a few million dollars, a few hundred thousand dollars, we should reflect on how to use the money to find solutions so that people in the world can live with each other. We must find solutions in the Middle East so that the Palestinians can also be recognized as men and women with a passport, so that Iran and Iraq can stop this unbelievably stupid war provided so gently by the billions of dollars of armaments they buy in the west.
Therefore, I will not blame the Hon. Member for obliging me to reflect on how we can find a solution. He is putting forward a very good resolution. He knows it will not take place, I regret to say, but at least he is putting something forward. He is obliging us to reflect and admit that the world is going crazy. Money, money, money. Nuclear submarines. Everyone says they want them built, but one person will say to build them in Quebec and another will say to build them in the Atlantic provinces.
As I look at my hon. friend from western Canada, the Hon. Member for Capliano (Mrs. Collins), who I know would like to participate in the debate, I think she would say: "No, no, they should be built in my part of the country''. But there should be some young people who say: "You politicians, instead of asking where will they be built, is there not one of you who will say, should they be built?"

That is important to me, Mr. Speaker. You see, they argue to find out who will build more and more, always more and enough to kill one another 1,000 times over. Well, I like people who say: Is there no alternative, could we not get together and try to find fresh approaches just so people will get better acquainted? I am one of those who passionately believe in what Mr. Gorbatchev is trying to do-and many of my colleagues will probably be shocked. Mr. Gorbatchev is advocating a major policy of glasnot, a policy of openness. I have very cynical colleagues in all political parties who tell me:

All this is bluff. I said last night to someone from the Soviet Embassy that if it is bluff, I call his bluff and we will see. If it is bluff, if it is not genuine, there will be politicians who will revert to the good old days of the cold war. But a Member of Parliament on a Friday afternoon before adjournment asks us to reflect on a proposal that is quite complicated-he must admit that himself. In order to force us to reflect, he has to propose something. This is what the Flon. Member has done. We could attack each other and be partisan about it. I did not want to answer Hon. Members who spoke point by point because, after all, we live in the British parliamentary system where people can and should have strong views on many issues. I, for one, instead of being partisan, want to thank the Hon. Member who made me stay here on a Friday afternoon, although in good company. Your company, Mr. Speaker, is always delightful, and I include the staff, the young pages and all my colleagues. I will reflect with the Hon. Member. Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have a chance to speak in support of this motion. 1 recognize that the time is running short, and I will do my best to leave a share of the time for the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) who, 1 understand, also wishes to speak.
The first point I wish to make is simply to reiterate the focus of this motion, which is 100 per cent tax credit to be transferred to a recognized international agency for peace. If it were enacted, this would be a democratic decision supported by a majority of Parliament, if it so decided, presumably with the backing of a majority of people in this country, and channeled into things that were recognized as peace activities. It would not be the whim of a private individual. However, what this proposal does is to raise a principle of the individual conscience, and of the right of the individual, which has a long history in western culture and in what we call our democratic tradition
In 1709, for example, the Quaker colony of Pennsylvania was ordered by the British Crown to provide funds toward the cost of an invasion of what we might have called French Canada. The Quaker colony of Pennsylvania refused to provide the money. I do not know the details, but I would imagine that in 1709 some Canadian lives were not lost because the Quaker colony of Pennsylvania refused what was then a lawful order of the monarch of Britain. What happened to the Quakers when they did that, I do not know. A couple of generations later there was a revolution in the Thirteen Colonies. I believe that Canada benefited because those Quakers disobeyed the British monarch.
Peace-making
Earlier there is the tradition that St. Hugh of Lincoln disobeyed one of the most famous British kings, Richard the Lion-Hearted, because Richard wanted money to go and make war against France. Whatever money St. Hugh of Lincoln did not give to Richard the Lion-Hearted, although he was disobeying the law and the king, probably saved some lives. We do not know whose ancestors those were, but I am glad that he did it. I am glad that there are those examples, and there are many others in history.
They have continued to the point where Archbishop Hantausen of Seattle in the United States has been charged with refusing to pay his taxes. He looks out of the window of his archiepiscopal office at the Trident submarine in the bay in front of him and he states, "That is offensive to human beings and to God. I will not give my share of my money to finance such an offence". He is breaking the law, but he is prepared to suffer for it. I thank God that there are people like that. Some people are in a position to do that directly. Many of us with tax deductions do not know how we could do it if we so decided, but at least this suggests the beginning of a development of that principle.
I want to move on to point out why people in a modern society may feel that the only equivalent they have to refusal to bear arms-which is a tradition that we do honour. We do exempt people who conscientiously refuse to bear arms-and why others say that their way of being forced to share in the killing is through their taxes.
This week many of us had the benefit and the pleasure of meeting with Veterans Against Nuclear Arms. This is an organization of Canadian veterans, many of whom served with distinction as officers, some of whom were decorated in World War II and in other wars.
They have asked us to consider the principle that the defence paper of the Hon. Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) leads us into serious errors, for example, when it talks about having stable mutual deterrence through nuclear weapons. They point out that, with the airborne sea-launched and ground-launched long range cruise missiles, the Trident II and Typhoon submarines, the MX missile, and the planned Midget Man missile, the BI bomber, and so on, we do not have stable deterrence. We have more and more unstable deterrence. The refusal to help in building those is an act in defence not only of the safety of some foreigners, it is an act in the defence of the safety of Canadians. We would be the meat in the sandwich if there was a nuclear war.
The Veterans Against Nuclear Arms have also pointed out that the defence policy proposed completely ignores the United Nations. It abrogates blind support of NATO, ignoring the fact that NATO in its foundation undertook to be subordinate to the United Nations. One of the principles in its charter is that differences shall be negotiated rather than settled by force. That peaceful principle of negotiation has been ignored

Peace-making
by NATO, and the United Nations is ignored by Canada's defence policy.
This week those veterans spent their time coming to Ottawa to remind us of some of our basic peace traditions. I believe that, whether they agree or not with this peace tax proposal, they are recalling us in the same way as did the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly), and the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme). On one point, I would even agree with the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson). If somebody stated that they did not want their money to go to an abortion clinic, but that they wanted it to be spent on family planning education or family planning facilitation, I could accept that. I think that that would be a sound way of allowing serious differences of conscience on important matters.
I hope that this peace tax proposal will be given serious thought by Members of Parliament on all sides.

speechtext:
In the few minutes left this afternoon to speak on this Private Member's Motion, I would like to make a few comments. In putting forward the motion, the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) deals with two different issues. The first would allow for individual taxpayers to reallocate some portion of their income tax which would ordinarily go for defence purposes, and instead give it to peace organizations or those involved in overseas development.
In that respect, I cannot agree with the motion. We are all in agreement with finding ways to promote peace around the world. For many of us, that was one of the underlying reasons that we wanted to serve the Canadian public and be part of the parliamentary process. To provide a system such as the peace tax, as the Hon. Member proposes, would, in my mind, lead to financial chaos.
In our parliamentary system, usually once every four years, Parties put forward their programs, and suggest what their priorities will be and how they plan to allocate funds during the time that they are in office. The public is then aware and participates in a whole variety of ways in the development of legislative processes, as we had with the Budget yesterday, and that is the way that we decide on these types of issues and on the appropriate priorities.
1 know that my hon. colleagues from another Party will have different ideas about how we should allocate tax money and
have different priorities, as perhaps would Members on this side of the House. But to allow individual taxpayers to make their own decision, to have a shopping list on the income tax form where they check off if they believe in agricultural payments, or that they do not like this item, would not be a workable solution.
The recent court decision mentioned by my colleague upholds that point of view. In that decision, Federal Court Justice George Addy stated that this type of approach would lead to chaos. He told Dr. Jerilynn Prior:
There are practical obstacles to allowing Prior to withhold payment of taxes for defence purposes.
One can easily envisage government actions and policies-to which certain taxpayers and possibly a great number of taxpayers might conscientiously and out of deep and sincere moral and religious convictions, consider to be totally wrong, reprehensible, unjustified and even evil-
Justice Addy further stated:
One such issue on which public attention is being focused today is the extremely divisive question of whether public money should be expended for abortions.
If each taxpayer who might be conscientiously objecting to this policy was entitled by law to withhold a percentage of income tax, complete chaos would result and orderly government would break down.
Justice Addy went on to say:
-even if someone found that Prior's freedom of conscience was infringed by paying taxes for military purposes, the infringement would probably be justified as reasonable under Section 1 of the Charter, which guarantees the rights set out in it subject only to such reasonable limits prescribed by law as can be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society.
Certainly, in my mind, this is an instance where that provision would come into play.
I had hoped to have a chance to talk about my own view of peace-making, but perhaps there will be a further opportunity to debate that issue.
